The figures of the sum-total showed a row of *0*’s long enough to allow Guillaume for once to relax the stern rule as to dessert which reigned throughout the year. The shrewd old draper rubbed his hands, and allowed his assistants to remain at table. The members of the crew had hardly swallowed their thimbleful of some homemade liqueur, when the rumble of a carriage was heard. The family party were going to see *Cendrillon* at the Variétés, while the two younger apprentices each received a crown of six francs, with permission to go wherever they chose, provided they were in by midnight.
Notwithstanding this debauch, the old cloth-merchant was shaving himself at six next morning, put on his maroon-colored coat, of which the glowing lights afforded him perennial enjoyment, fastened a pair of gold buckles on the knee-straps of his ample satin breeches; and then, at about seven o’clock, while all were still sleeping in the house, he made his way to the little office adjoining the shop on the first floor. Daylight came in through a window, fortified by iron bars, and looking out on a small yard surrounded by such black walls that it was very like a well. The old merchant opened the iron-lined shutters, which were so familiar to him, and threw up the lower half of the sash window. The icy air of the courtyard came in to cool the hot atmosphere of the little room, full of the odor peculiar to offices.
The merchant remained standing, his hand resting on the greasy arm of a large cane chair lined with morocco, of which the original hue had disappeared; he seemed to hesitate as to seating himself. He looked with affection at the double desk, where his wife’s seat, opposite his own, was fitted into a little niche in the wall. He contemplated the numbered boxes, the files, the implements, the cash box﻿—objects all of immemorial origin, and fancied himself in the room with the shade of Master Chevrel. He even pulled out the high stool on which he had once sat in the presence of his departed master. This stool, covered with black leather, the horsehair showing at every corner﻿—as it had long done, without, however, coming out﻿—he placed with a shaking hand on the very spot where his predecessor had put it, and then, with an emotion difficult to describe, he pulled a bell, which rang at the head of Joseph Lebas’ bed.

===Chinese===

总计的数字显示出一长排「0」，长得足以让纪尧姆破天荒松弛一下全年统治着的关于甜点的严规。精明的老呢绒商搓着双手，允许伙计们留在桌旁。船员们刚把一小盅家酿利口酒咽下去，门外便响起马车轱辘声。全家要上杂耍剧院看《灰姑娘》去；两个年轻的学徒每人领到一枚六法郎的埃居，获准随意去玩，只要半夜前回店。
尽管有这样一场放浪，第二天早晨六点，老呢绒商已经在刮脸了；他穿上那件枣红色外衣——衣料的光泽年年给他享受不尽——在宽大的缎面短裤的膝扣带上系好一对金搭扣；然后，七点钟光景，趁全家还在酣睡，他走进紧挨二楼店铺的小账房。日光从一扇加固了铁条的窗子透进来，窗子对着一个小院，四周是黑黢黢的高墙，活像一口井。老商人打开他再熟悉不过的包铁板窗，推起窗子的下半扇。院子里冰冷的空气涌进来，给这间弥漫着账房特有气味的小屋降降温。
商人站着，一只手搭在一张蒙摩洛哥皮的大藤椅油亮的扶手上——皮子本来的颜色早已褪尽；他仿佛迟疑着不肯坐下。他深情地望着那张对坐的斜面双人账台，妻子的座位正对着他自己的，嵌在墙上的一个小龛里。他端详着编了号的匣子、文件夹、器具、钱箱——一切都是年代久远的老物件，恍惚间只当谢弗勒尔师傅的亡魂正与他同室。他甚至拉出了那张高凳——当年他就坐在上面，侍立于已故东家的面前。凳面蒙着黑皮，四角都露着马鬃——早就露了，倒也从来没有脱出来——他用颤抖的手把它放在前任当年放的同一个位置上，然后怀着难以言表的激动，拉了一下铃：那铃，就吊在约瑟夫·勒巴的床头。

===Original===

When this decisive blow had been struck, the old man, for whom, no doubt, these reminiscences were too much, took up three or four bills of exchange, and looked at them without seeing them.
Suddenly Joseph Lebas stood before him.
“Sit down there,” said Guillaume, pointing to the stool.
As the old master draper had never yet bid his assistant be seated in his presence, Joseph Lebas was startled.
“What do you think of these notes?” asked Guillaume.
“They will never be paid.”
“Why?”
“Well, I heard the day before yesterday Étienne and Co. had made their payments in gold.”
“Oh, oh!” said the draper. “Well, one must be very ill to show one’s bile. Let us speak of something else.﻿—Joseph, the stocktaking is done.”
“Yes, monsieur, and the dividend is one of the best you have ever made.”
“Do not use newfangled words. Say the profits, Joseph. Do you know, my boy, that this result is partly owing to you? And I do not intend to pay you a salary any longer. Madame Guillaume has suggested to me to take you into partnership.﻿—‘Guillaume and Lebas’; will not that make a good business name? We might add, ‘and Co.’ to round off the firm’s signature.”
Tears rose to the eyes of Joseph Lebas, who tried to hide them.
“Oh, Monsieur Guillaume, how have I deserved such kindness? I only do my duty. It was so much already that you should take an interest in a poor orph﻿—”
He was brushing the cuff of his left sleeve with his right hand, and dared not look at the old man, who smiled as he thought that this modest young fellow no doubt needed, as he had needed once on a time, some encouragement to complete his explanation.
“To be sure,” said Virginie’s father, “you do not altogether deserve this favor, Joseph. You have not so much confidence in me as I have in you.” (The young man looked up quickly.) “You know all the secrets of the cashbox. For the last two years I have told you almost all my concerns. I have sent you to travel in our goods. In short, I have nothing on my conscience as regards you. But you﻿—you have a soft place, and you have never breathed a word of it.” Joseph Lebas blushed. “Ah, ha!” cried Guillaume, “so you thought you could deceive an old fox like me? When you knew that I had scented the Lecocq bankruptcy?”
“What, monsieur?” replied Joseph Lebas, looking at his master as keenly as his master looked at him, “you knew that I was in love?”

===Chinese===

这决定性的一击敲过之后，老人——这些回忆对他说来无疑太过沉重了——拿起三四张汇票，看着它们，却什么也没看进去。
忽然，约瑟夫·勒巴已站在他面前。
「坐那儿吧。」纪尧姆指着那张凳子说。
老呢绒商东家还从来不曾让伙计在自己面前坐过，约瑟夫·勒巴不由一惊。
「您看这几张票子怎么样？」纪尧姆问。
「永远不会兑付的。」
「为什么？」
「这个——前天我听说艾蒂安公司拿金币付款了。」
「哦，哦！」呢绒商说，「唉，人病得厉害，胆汁才会上脸。咱们说别的吧。——约瑟夫，盘货盘完了。」
「是的，先生，这次的红利是您历年最好的一次。」
「别用那些新字眼。说利润，约瑟夫。你可知道，孩子，这成绩有一部分是你的功劳？从今往后我不打算再付你薪水了。纪尧姆太太向我提议，让你入伙。——『纪尧姆–勒巴商号』；这商号名头还不响亮吗？咱们还可以加上『公司』二字，把商号的署名凑得圆圆满满。」
约瑟夫·勒巴眼里涌上泪水，竭力忍着。
「哦，纪尧姆先生，我何德何能，受您这样的恩典？我不过是尽本分。您肯关照一个可怜的孤——」
他用右手拂着左袖的袖口，不敢看老人。老人微微一笑，心想这个腼腆的年轻人，无疑正像自己当年一样，需要一点鼓励才把话说完。
「话虽如此，」维尔日妮的父亲说，「你也并不全然当得起这份厚爱，约瑟夫。你对我的信任，可比不上我对你的。」（年轻人猛地抬起头。）「钱箱的秘密你全知道。两年来，我的事几乎样样都告诉你了。我派你出门跑过我们的货。总之，我对你问心无愧。可是你——你心里有一块软地方，却从来没有向我吐露过一个字。」约瑟夫·勒巴脸红了。「啊哈！」纪尧姆喊道，「你当你能瞒过我这只老狐狸？你明明知道我早嗅出了勒科克商号要倒闭？」
「怎么，先生？」约瑟夫·勒巴答道，用东家打量他的那种锐利目光回望着东家，「您知道我恋爱了？」

===Original===

“I know everything, you rascal,” said the worthy and cunning old merchant, pulling the assistant’s ear. “And I forgive you﻿—I did the same myself.”
“And you will give her to me?”
“Yes﻿—with fifty thousand crowns; and I will leave you as much by will, and we will start on our new career under the name of a new firm. We will do good business yet, my boy!” added the old man, getting up and flourishing his arms. “I tell you, son-in-law, there is nothing like trade. Those who ask what pleasure is to be found in it are simpletons. To be on the scent of a good bargain, to hold your own on ’Change, to watch as anxiously as at the gaming-table whether Étienne and Co. will fail or no, to see a regiment of Guards march past all dressed in your cloth, to trip your neighbor up﻿—honestly of course!﻿—to make the goods cheaper than others can; then to carry out an undertaking which you have planned, which begins, grows, totters, and succeeds! to know the workings of every house of business as well as a minister of police, so as never to make a mistake; to hold up your head in the midst of wrecks, to have friends by correspondence in every manufacturing town; is not that a perpetual game, Joseph? That is life, that is! I shall die in that harness, like old Chevrel, but taking it easy now, all the same.”
In the heat of his eager rhetoric, old Guillaume had scarcely looked at his assistant, who was weeping copiously. “Why, Joseph, my poor boy, what is the matter?”
“Oh, I love her so! Monsieur Guillaume, that my heart fails me; I believe﻿—”
“Well, well, boy,” said the old man, touched, “you are happier than you know, by God! For she loves you. I know it.”
And he blinked his little green eyes as he looked at the young man.
“Mademoiselle Augustine! Mademoiselle Augustine!” exclaimed Joseph Lebas in his rapture.
He was about to rush out of the room when he felt himself clutched by a hand of iron, and his astonished master spun him round in front of him once more.
“What has Augustine to do with this matter?” he asked, in a voice which instantly froze the luckless Joseph.
“Is it not she that﻿—that﻿—I love?” stammered the assistant.
Much put out by his own want of perspicacity, Guillaume sat down again, and rested his long head in his hands to consider the perplexing situation in which he found himself. Joseph Lebas, shamefaced and in despair, remained standing.

===Chinese===

「我什么都知道，你这个滑头，」这位可敬而狡黠的老商人说着，扯了扯伙计的耳朵。「我饶了你——当年我自己也一样。」
「您肯把她给我？」
「肯——陪嫁五万埃居；遗嘱里我还要留给你同样一笔；咱们就以新商号的名义开始新的事业。咱们还能大干一场呢，孩子！」老人站起来，挥舞着两条胳膊又说，「我告诉你，女婿，天底下什么也比不上做买卖。问做买卖有什么乐趣的人都是傻子。嗅到一笔好生意，在交易所里寸步不让，像守着赌桌一样提心吊胆地盯着艾蒂安公司到底倒不倒，看着一团近卫军穿着你的呢料齐步走过，绊邻居一跤——当然是正大光明地绊！——把货做得比别人便宜；再把你筹划的一番事业办成，它起步、壮大、摇晃、成功！把每一家商号的底细摸得像警务大臣一样清楚，永远不吃亏；在一片残骸中间昂起头来，在每一座制造业城市都有通信的朋友；约瑟夫，这难道不是一场没完没了的游戏吗？这才叫生活，就是这个！我要像老谢弗勒尔一样，套着这驾辕到死，不过从今往后可以清闲些了。」
老纪尧姆说得兴头上来，几乎没顾上看一眼伙计——那伙计早已泪如泉涌。「咦，约瑟夫，我可怜的孩子，你怎么了？」
「哦，我太爱她了！纪尧姆先生，我一想这心里就发慌；我觉得——」
「好了，好了，孩子，」老人被打动了，「你比自己知道的还幸福，天哪！因为她爱你。这我知道。」
他望着年轻人，眨着那双绿莹莹的小眼睛。
「奥古斯丁小姐！奥古斯丁小姐！」约瑟夫·勒巴欣喜若狂地喊道。
他正要冲出房门，却被一只铁腕攥住，惊愕的东家把他一把又拽回面前。
「这件事跟奥古斯丁有什么相干？」他问，那声音顿时把不幸的约瑟夫冻住了。
「我爱的——难道不是她——不是她吗？」伙计结结巴巴地说。
纪尧姆懊恼自己眼力不济，重新坐下，双手托着那颗长脑袋，琢磨起自己陷入的这桩乱局。约瑟夫·勒巴羞愧绝望，站在一旁。

===Original===

“Joseph,” the draper said with frigid dignity, “I was speaking of Virginie. Love cannot be made to order, I know. I know, too, that you can be trusted. We will forget all this. I will not let Augustine marry before Virginie.﻿—Your interest will be ten percent.”
The young man, to whom love gave I know not what power of courage and eloquence, clasped his hand, and spoke in his turn﻿—spoke for a quarter of an hour, with so much warmth and feeling, that he altered the situation. If the question had been a matter of business the old tradesman would have had fixed principles to guide his decision; but, tossed a thousand miles from commerce, on the ocean of sentiment, without a compass, he floated, as he told himself, undecided in the face of such an unexpected event. Carried away by his fatherly kindness, he began to beat about the bush.
“Deuce take it, Joseph, you must know that there are ten years between my two children. Mademoiselle Chevrel was no beauty, still she has had nothing to complain of in me. Do as I did. Come, come, don’t cry. Can you be so silly? What is to be done? It can be managed perhaps. There is always some way out of a scrape. And we men are not always devoted Celadons to our wives﻿—you understand? Madame Guillaume is very pious.﻿ ﻿… Come. By Gad, boy, give your arm to Augustine this morning as we go to Mass.”
These were the phrases spoken at random by the old draper, and their conclusion made the lover happy. He was already thinking of a friend of his as a match for Mademoiselle Virginie, as he went out of the smoky office, pressing his future father-in-law’s hand, after saying with a knowing look that all would turn out for the best.
“What will Madame Guillaume say to it?” was the idea that greatly troubled the worthy merchant when he found himself alone.
At breakfast Madame Guillaume and Virginie, to whom the draper had not yet confided his disappointment, cast meaning glances at Joseph Lebas, who was extremely embarrassed. The young assistant’s bashfulness commended him to his mother-in-law’s good graces. The matron became so cheerful that she smiled as she looked at her husband, and allowed herself some little pleasantries of time-honored acceptance in such simple families. She wondered whether Joseph or Virginie were the taller, to ask them to compare their height.

===Chinese===

「约瑟夫，」呢绒商带着冷冰冰的尊严说，「我说的是维尔日妮。我知道，爱情不能按单订制。我也知道你靠得住。这层咱们就揭过去吧。我不能让奥古斯丁先于维尔日妮出嫁。——你的股份占一成。」
爱情给了这年轻人不知怎样的勇气与口才，他握住东家的手，轮到他来说了——一刻钟滔滔不绝，说得那样热烈、那样动情，竟把局面扭转了。倘若问题出在生意上，老商人自有铁定的原则给他拿主意；可是被抛出买卖场一千里，漂在情感的大洋上，没有罗盘，用他自己的话说，面对这样一桩意外，他只有随波逐流，拿不定主意。慈父的心肠一冲动，他开始旁敲侧击。
「该死，约瑟夫，你可知道我两个闺女差着十岁。谢弗勒尔小姐当年算不上美人，可她跟着我也没有什么可抱怨的。照我那样做就是了。好了，好了，别哭了。怎么这样傻？有什么办法呢？兴许有法子通融。天无绝人之路。再说咱们这些做丈夫的，对老婆也不见得个个都是痴情的塞拉东——你明白吗？纪尧姆太太是很虔诚的。……去吧。天哪，孩子，今天早晨望弥撒，你就把胳膊伸给奥古斯丁吧。」
老呢绒商东一句西一句地信口说着，结论那一句却叫情人喜出望外。走出那间烟雾缭绕的账房时，他已琢磨着把一个朋友配给维尔日妮小姐了；他意味深长地说一切都会圆满，一面紧握着未来岳父的手。
「纪尧姆太太会怎么说呢？」这是可敬的商人独自留下时最犯愁的念头。
早餐时，纪尧姆太太和维尔日妮——呢绒商还没有向她们吐露自己的失望——朝约瑟夫·勒巴丢去意味深长的眼色，后者窘得不得了。年轻伙计的腼腆却讨得了丈母娘的欢心。主妇快活起来，竟微笑着望了望丈夫，还容许自己开了几句在这样的朴实人家世代通行的玩笑。她说不定是约瑟夫高还是维尔日妮高，要他们背对背比比个子。

===Original===

This preliminary fooling brought a cloud to the master’s brow, and he even made such a point of decorum that he desired Augustine to take the assistant’s arm on their way to Saint-Leu. Madame Guillaume, surprised at this manly delicacy, honored her husband with a nod of approval. So the procession left the house in such order as to suggest no suspicious meaning to the neighbors.
“Does it not seem to you, Mademoiselle Augustine,” said the assistant, and he trembled, “that the wife of a merchant whose credit is as good as Monsieur Guillaume’s, for instance, might enjoy herself a little more than Madame your mother does? Might wear diamonds﻿—or keep a carriage? For my part, if I were to marry, I should be glad to take all the work, and see my wife happy. I would not put her into the countinghouse. In the drapery business, you see, a woman is not so necessary now as formerly. Monsieur Guillaume was quite right to act as he did﻿—and besides, his wife liked it. But so long as a woman knows how to turn her hand to the bookkeeping, the correspondence, the retail business, the orders, and her housekeeping, so as not to sit idle, that is enough. At seven o’clock, when the shop is shut, I shall take my pleasures, go to the play, and into company.﻿—But you are not listening to me.”
“Yes, indeed, Monsieur Joseph. What do you think of painting? That is a fine calling.”
“Yes. I know a master house-painter, Monsieur Lourdois. He is well-to-do.”
Thus conversing, the family reached the Church of Saint-Leu. There Madame Guillaume reasserted her rights, and, for the first time, placed Augustine next herself, Virginie taking her place on the fourth chair, next to Lebas. During the sermon all went well between Augustine and Thédore, who, standing behind a pillar, worshiped his Madonna with fervent devotion; but at the elevation of the Host, Madame Guillaume discovered, rather late, that her daughter Augustine was holding her prayerbook upside down. She was about to speak to her strongly, when, lowering her veil, she interrupted her own devotions to look in the direction where her daughter’s eyes found attraction. By the help of her spectacles she saw the young artist, whose fashionable elegance seemed to proclaim him a cavalry officer on leave rather than a tradesman of the neighborhood.

===Chinese===

这场开场玩笑给东家的额头蒙上了阴云；他甚至把体面做足到这般地步：吩咐去圣勒乌的路上由奥古斯丁挽伙计的手臂。纪尧姆太太对这份男子汉的细腻暗暗吃惊，郑重地向丈夫点了点头，以示嘉许。于是这一行人出门了，次序井然，左邻右舍看不出半点可疑的名堂。
「奥古斯丁小姐，您不觉得吗，」伙计说，声音发着抖，「一个信用像纪尧姆先生这样好的商人的太太，比方说，本可以过得比令堂快活一点？可以戴钻石——或者养一辆马车？要是我结了婚，我情愿一个人担下全部营生，看着太太快活。我不会把她安在账房里。您瞧，如今做呢绒生意，女人不比从前那么少不了了。纪尧姆先生当年的做法完全对——何况师娘自己也乐意。不过，一个女人只要懂得记账、写信、照应门市、接订货、理家务，闲不着手，也就够了。到七点钟铺子上了门板，我就去找乐子，看戏，会朋友。——可您没有在听我讲。」
「在听呢，约瑟夫先生。您对绘画怎么看？那可是个好行当。」
「是不错。我认得一个房屋漆匠师傅，卢尔杜瓦先生。他日子过得挺富裕。」
一家人就这样说着话，到了圣勒乌教堂。在那里，纪尧姆太太重新行使起她的权威，第一次把奥古斯丁安置在自己身边，维尔日妮则坐到第四把椅子上，挨着勒巴。讲道的时候，奥古斯丁和泰奥多尔之间一切顺利；他立在柱子后面，以炽热的虔诚礼拜他的圣母。可是举扬圣体的时候，纪尧姆太太——未免迟了些——发现女儿奥古斯丁把祈祷书拿倒了。她正要狠狠说她一句，一压面纱，竟打断了自己的祷告，朝女儿的眼睛被吸引的方向望去。借着眼镜，她看见了那个年轻艺术家：他那身时髦的潇洒，与其说像本街的买卖人，倒不如说像一个休假的骑兵军官。

===Original===

It is difficult to conceive of the state of violent agitation in which Madame Guillaume found herself﻿—she, who flattered herself on having brought up her daughters to perfection﻿—on discovering in Augustine a clandestine passion of which her prudery and ignorance exaggerated the perils. She believed her daughter to be cankered to the core.
“Hold your book right way up, miss,” she muttered in a low voice, tremulous with wrath. She snatched away the telltale prayerbook and returned it with the letterpress right way up. “Do not allow your eyes to look anywhere but at your prayers,” she added, “or I shall have something to say to you. Your father and I will talk to you after church.”
These words came like a thunderbolt on poor Augustine. She felt faint; but, torn between the distress she felt and the dread of causing a commotion in church she bravely concealed her anguish. It was, however, easy to discern the stormy state of her soul from the trembling of her prayerbook, and the tears which dropped on every page she turned. From the furious glare shot at him by Madame Guillaume the artist saw the peril into which his love affair had fallen; he went out, with a raging soul, determined to venture all.
“Go to your room, miss!” said Madame Guillaume, on their return home; “we will send for you, but take care not to quit it.”
The conference between the husband and wife was conducted so secretly that at first nothing was heard of it. Virginie, however, who had tried to give her sister courage by a variety of gentle remonstrances, carried her good nature so far as to listen at the door of her mother’s bedroom where the discussion was held, to catch a word or two. The first time she went down to the lower floor she heard her father exclaim, “Then, madame, do you wish to kill your daughter?”
“My poor dear!” said Virginie, in tears, “papa takes your part.”
“And what do they want to do to Thédore?” asked the innocent girl.
Virginie, inquisitive, went down again; but this time she stayed longer; she learned that Joseph Lebas loved Augustine. It was written that on this memorable day, this house, generally so peaceful, should be a hell. Monsieur Guillaume brought Joseph Lebas to despair by telling him of Augustine’s love for a stranger. Lebas, who had advised his friend to become a suitor for Mademoiselle Virginie, saw all his hopes wrecked.

===Chinese===

很难想象纪尧姆太太此刻激烈的激动——她自诩把两个女儿调教得完美无瑕，如今却在奥古斯丁身上发现了一段私情，她的假正经与无知更把其中的危险夸大了。她认定女儿已经烂到了芯子里。
「把书拿正了，小姐，」她低声呵斥，声音气得发抖。她一把夺过那本招供的祈祷书，把字面朝正了还给她。「不许你的眼睛往别处看，只许看你的祷文，」她又加一句，「不然我有话跟你说。做完礼拜，你父亲和我要找你谈话。」
这几句话对可怜的奥古斯丁不啻晴天霹雳。她几乎晕倒；但一边是心中的酸楚，一边是怕在教堂里闹出动静，她勇敢地把痛苦压了下去。不过，从她那本抖个不停的祈祷书上，从她翻过的每一页上落下的泪珠里，都不难看出她灵魂里的风暴。艺术家从纪尧姆太太朝他射来的狂怒目光里，看出自己的恋爱陷入了何等的险境；他走了出去，心头的怒火翻腾，决意孤注一掷。
「回你房里去，小姐！」回到家，纪尧姆太太说，「我们会叫你，你自己当心，别离开房门一步。」
夫妻之间的会谈进行得极其隐秘，起初一点风声也没有透出来。倒是维尔日妮，她已经用种种温柔的劝慰给妹妹打过气，好心干脆好到底，跑到举行讨论的母亲卧房门口偷听，想逮着一两个词。头一回下楼，她听见父亲喊道：「那么，太太，你是要逼死你的女儿吗？」
「我可怜的宝贝！」维尔日妮含着泪说，「爸爸是向着你的。」
「那他们要把泰奥多尔怎么样？」天真的姑娘问。
维尔日妮好奇心起，又下去了一趟；这一回待得久些；她得知约瑟夫·勒巴爱着奥古斯丁。天意注定，在这个难忘的日子里，这座素来安宁的宅子要变成一座地狱。纪尧姆先生把奥古斯丁爱上一个外人的事告诉约瑟夫·勒巴，使他陷入了绝望。勒巴曾劝他的朋友去求娶维尔日妮小姐，如今眼见一切希望都破灭了。

===Original===

Mademoiselle Virginie, overcome by hearing that Joseph had, in a way, refused her, had a sick headache. The dispute that had arisen from the discussion between Monsieur and Madame Guillaume, when, for the third time in their lives, they had been of antagonistic opinions, had shown itself in a terrible form. Finally, at half-past four in the afternoon, Augustine, pale, trembling, and with red eyes, was haled before her father and mother. The poor child artlessly related the too brief tale of her love. Reassured by a speech from her father, who promised to listen to her in silence, she gathered courage as she pronounced to her parents the name of Thédore de Sommervieux, with a mischievous little emphasis on the aristocratic *de*. And yielding to the unknown charm of talking of her feelings, she was brave enough to declare with innocent decision that she loved Monsieur de Sommervieux, that she had written to him, and she added, with tears in her eyes: “To sacrifice me to another man would make me wretched.”
“But, Augustine, you cannot surely know what a painter is?” cried her mother with horror.
“Madame Guillaume!” said the old man, compelling her to silence.﻿—“Augustine,” he went on, “artists are generally little better than beggars. They are too extravagant not to be always a bad sort. I served the late Monsieur Joseph Vernet, the late Monsieur Lekain, and the late Monsieur Noverre. Oh, if you could only know the tricks played on poor Father Chevrel by that Monsieur Noverre, by the Chevalier de Saint-Georges, and especially by Monsieur Philidor! They are a set of rascals; I know them well! They all have a gab and nice manners. Ah, your Monsieur Sumer﻿—, Somm﻿—”
“De Sommervieux, papa.”
“Well, well, de Sommervieux, well and good. He can never have been half so sweet to you as Monsieur le Chevalier de Saint-Georges was to me the day I got a verdict of the consuls against him. And in those days they were gentlemen of quality.”
“But, father, Monsieur Thédore is of good family, and he wrote me that he is rich; his father was called Chevalier de Sommervieux before the Revolution.”

===Chinese===

维尔日妮小姐听说约瑟夫等于回绝了她，一急，偏头痛发作了。纪尧姆先生和太太的这一场争执——这是他们平生第三次意见相左——以可怕的形式表现了出来。最后，下午四点半，奥古斯丁被带到父母面前：脸色苍白，浑身发抖，眼睛通红。可怜的孩子天真地讲了她那段短得可怜的恋爱史。父亲许诺静听不语，一句宽慰的话壮了她的胆，她向父母说出泰奥多尔·德·索默维厄的名字，念到那个贵族气的「德」字时还淘气地加重了一点。接着她尝到了倾诉衷肠的从未领略的甜头，竟勇敢地以天真的决断宣布：她爱德·索默维厄先生，她给他写过信；她还噙着眼泪补上一句：「把我牺牲给另一个男人，会叫我痛苦一辈子的。」
「可是，奥古斯丁，你总不会知道画家是什么东西吧？」母亲恐怖地喊道。
「纪尧姆太太！」老头子喝住她。——「奥古斯丁，」他接着说，「艺术家多半比叫花子强不了多少。他们挥霍成性，不可能是什么好人。我伺候过已故的约瑟夫·韦尔内先生、已故的勒凯恩先生、已故的诺韦尔先生。咳，你要是知道那位诺韦尔先生、圣乔治骑士，尤其是菲里多尔先生，在可怜的谢弗勒尔老爹身上耍过多少花招就好了！那是一伙无赖；我太了解他们了！个个都能说会道、举止文雅。嗐，你那位苏麦——，索麦——」
「德·索默维厄，爸爸。」
「好好，德·索默维厄，就这么叫吧。他待你再甜，也甜不过圣乔治骑士当年待我——我可是拿到执政裁决赢了他的官司的。那时候，人家可是有身份的体面人。」
「可是，爸爸，泰奥多尔先生出身好人家，他写信告诉我他很有钱；他父亲在大革命前就称作索默维厄骑士。

===Original===

At these words Monsieur Guillaume looked at his terrible better half, who, like an angry woman, sat tapping the floor with her foot while keeping sullen silence; she avoided even casting wrathful looks at Augustine, appearing to leave to Monsieur Guillaume the whole responsibility in so grave a matter, since her opinion was not listened to. Nevertheless, in spite of her apparent self-control, when she saw her husband giving way so mildly under a catastrophe which had no concern with business, she exclaimed:
“Really, monsieur, you are so weak with your daughters! However﻿—”
The sound of a carriage, which stopped at the door, interrupted the rating which the old draper already quaked at. In a minute Madame Roguin was standing in the middle of the room, and looking at the actors in this domestic scene: “I know all, my dear cousin,” said she, with a patronizing air.
Madame Roguin made the great mistake of supposing that a Paris notary’s wife could play the part of a favorite of fashion.
“I know all,” she repeated, “and I have come into Noah’s Ark, like the dove, with the olive-branch. I read that allegory in the *Genie du Christianisme*,” she added, turning to Madame Guillaume; “the allusion ought to please you, cousin. Do you know,” she went on, smiling at Augustine, “that Monsieur de Sommervieux is a charming man? He gave me my portrait this morning, painted by a master’s hand. It is worth at least six thousand francs.” And at these words she patted Monsieur Guillaume on the arm. The old draper could not help making a grimace with his lips, which was peculiar to him.
“I know Monsieur de Sommervieux very well,” the Dove ran on. “He has come to my evenings this fortnight past, and made them delightful. He has told me all his woes, and commissioned me to plead for him. I know since this morning that he adores Augustine, and he shall have her. Ah, cousin, do not shake your head in refusal. He will be created Baron, I can tell you, and has just been made Chevalier of the Legion of Honor, by the Emperor himself, at the Salon. Roguin is now his lawyer, and knows all his affairs. Well! Monsieur de Sommervieux has twelve thousand francs a year in good landed estate. Do you know that the father-in-law of such a man may get a rise in life﻿—be mayor of his arrondissement, for instance.

===Chinese===

听了这话，纪尧姆先生望了望他那位令人生畏的内当家；她像一个生闷气的女人，坐着用脚点地，板着脸一言不发；她甚至不肯朝奥古斯丁瞪一眼，摆出把这桩大事的全部责任都推给纪尧姆先生的架势——反正她的话没人听。话虽如此，她表面克制，待看到丈夫在这场与买卖毫不相干的灾祸面前竟这样软弱退让，还是嚷了出来：
「说真的，先生，您对女儿们太软弱了！不过——」
一辆马车在门口停下的声音，打断了老呢绒商已经发怵的这场数落。转眼间，罗甘太太已站在客厅中央，环视着这幕家庭剧的众角色：「我全知道了，亲爱的表妹，」她摆出恩主的气派说。
罗甘太太犯了个大错：她以为巴黎一个公证人的太太，能扮演沙龙红人的角色。
「我全知道了，」她重复道，「我像鸽子一样进了诺亚方舟，嘴里衔着橄榄枝。这个典故我是从《基督教真谛》里读来的，」她转向纪尧姆太太补了一句，「这个影射该中您的意吧，表姐。您可知道，」她微笑着对奥古斯丁说下去，「德·索默维厄先生是个迷人的人？他今天早晨送了我一幅我的肖像，出自名家之手。至少值六千法郎呢。」说着她拍了拍纪尧姆先生的手臂。老呢绒商不禁做了个他特有的撇嘴的怪相。
「我同德·索默维厄先生很熟，」这位「鸽子」滔滔不绝，「这两个礼拜，他天天来我的晚会，把晚会点缀得妙不可言。他向我倾诉了他全部的苦恼，委托我替他说情。今天早晨我知道了他爱慕奥古斯丁，他一定能得到她。嗳，表姐，别摇头拒绝。我告诉您，他就要封男爵了，而且刚刚在沙龙上由皇帝亲口授予了荣誉军团骑士衔。罗甘如今是他的律师，他的事全知道。嘿！德·索默维厄先生每年有一万二千法郎上好的地产收益。您想想，这样一个人的岳父，说不定还能高升呢——比方说，当上区里的市长。

===Original===

Have we not seen Monsieur Dupont become a Count of the Empire, and a senator, all because he went as mayor to congratulate the Emperor on his entry into Vienna? Oh, this marriage must take place! For my part, I adore the dear young man. His behavior to Augustine is only met with in romances. Be easy, little one, you shall be happy, and every girl will wish she were in your place. Madame la Duchesse de Carigliano, who comes to my ‘At Homes,’ raves about Monsieur de Sommervieux. Some spiteful people say she only comes to me to meet him; as if a duchesse of yesterday was doing too much honor to a Chevrel, whose family have been respected citizens these hundred years!
“Augustine,” Madame Roguin went on, after a short pause, “I have seen the portrait. Heavens! How lovely it is! Do you know that the Emperor wanted to have it? He laughed, and said to the Deputy High Constable that if there were many women like that in his court while all the kings visited it, he should have no difficulty about preserving the peace of Europe. Is not that a compliment?”
The tempests with which the day had begun were to resemble those of nature, by ending in clear and serene weather. Madame Roguin displayed so much address in her harangue, she was able to touch so many strings in the dry hearts of Monsieur and Madame Guillaume, that at last she hit on one which she could work upon. At this strange period commerce and finance were more than ever possessed by the crazy mania for seeking alliance with rank; and the generals of the Empire took full advantage of this desire. Monsieur Guillaume, as a singular exception, opposed this deplorable craving. His favorite axioms were that, to secure happiness, a woman must marry a man of her own class; that everyone was punished sooner or later for having climbed too high; that love could so little endure under the worries of a household, that both husband and wife needed sound good qualities to be happy, that it would not do for one to be far in advance of the other, because, above everything, they must understand each other; if a man spoke Greek and his wife Latin, they might come to die of hunger. He had himself invented this sort of adage. And he compared such marriages to old-fashioned materials of mixed silk and wool.

===Chinese===

咱们不是都见着了吗：杜邦先生就因为当市长去恭贺皇帝驾临维也纳，竟当上了帝国的伯爵和元老？哦，这门亲事非成不可！要我说，我真爱慕这位可爱的年轻人。他待奥古斯丁的情意，只在小说里才见得到。放心吧，小宝贝，你会幸福的，家家姑娘都要羡慕你的命呢。卡里利亚诺公爵夫人常来我家做客，把德·索默维厄先生夸上了天。有些促狭鬼说，她上我家只为碰见他；仿佛一位昨儿个才封的公爵夫人光临谢弗勒尔家的门庭，还委屈了她似的——谢弗勒尔家可是百年来受人敬重的体面市民！
「奥古斯丁，」罗甘太太略停了停，又往下说，「那幅肖像我见过了。天哪！多美啊！你可知道皇帝都想要它？他笑着说，对宫廷大总管说，倘若在他那万王来朝的宫廷里多几位这样的女子，他保全欧洲的和平就不费吹灰之力了。这还不够恭维吗？」
这一天的开端虽是狂风暴雨，到头来竟也像大自然的雷雨一样，收梢在晴朗宁静的天空里。罗甘太太那一套说辞何等圆熟，纪尧姆先生和纪尧姆太太干涸的心上，多少根弦都被她拨到了，最后终于给她摸着了一根使得动的。在那个奇怪的时代，买卖和金融界比任何时候都更犯着攀结爵位的疯狂热病；帝国的将军们把这种心思利用了个够。纪尧姆先生却是个少有的例外，反对这可悲的痴念。他心爱的格言是：女人要保住幸福，必须嫁个同一阶层的男人；爬得太高的人，迟早要受惩罚；爱情在家务的烦扰之下经不起磕碰，所以夫妻要幸福，两个人都得有扎实的好品性；一个比另一个高出太多也不行，因为头一条便是两人要彼此听得懂——丈夫说希腊话，太太说拉丁话，两个到头来非饿死不可。这类格言就是他自己发明的。他还把这种婚姻比作旧时丝毛混纺的料子。

===Original===

Still, there is so much vanity at the bottom of man’s heart that the prudence of the pilot who steered the Cat and Racket so wisely gave way before Madame Roguin’s aggressive volubility. Austere Madame Guillaume was the first to see in her daughter’s affection a reason for abdicating her principles and for consenting to receive Monsieur de Sommervieux, whom she promised herself she would put under severe inquisition.
The old draper went to look for Joseph Lebas, and inform him of the state of affairs. At half-past six, the dining-room immortalized by the artist saw, united under its skylight, Monsieur and Madame Roguin, the young painter and his charming Augustine, Joseph Lebas, who found his happiness in patience, and Mademoiselle Virginie, convalescent from her headache. Monsieur and Madame Guillaume saw in perspective both their children married, and the fortunes of the Cat and Racket once more in skilful hands. Their satisfaction was at its height when, at dessert, Thédore made them a present of the wonderful picture which they had failed to see, representing the interior of the old shop, and to which they all owed so much happiness.
“Isn’t it pretty!” cried Guillaume. “And to think that anyone would pay thirty thousand francs for that!”
“Because you can see my lappets in it,” said Madame Guillaume.
“And the cloth unrolled!” added Lebas; “you might take it up in your hand.”
“Drapery always comes out well,” replied the painter. “We should be only too happy, we modern artists, if we could touch the perfection of antique drapery.”
“So you like drapery!” cried old Guillaume. “Well, then, by Gad! shake hands on that, my young friend. Since you can respect trade, we shall understand each other. And why should it be despised? The world began with trade, since Adam sold Paradise for an apple. He did not strike a good bargain though!” And the old man roared with honest laughter, encouraged by the champagne, which he sent round with a liberal hand. The band that covered the young artist’s eyes was so thick that he thought his future parents amiable. He was not above enlivening them by a few jests in the best taste. So he too pleased everyone.

===Chinese===

话虽如此，人心底里终究埋着那么多虚荣，把猫打球号掌得那样稳的那位领航员的谨慎，在罗甘太太咄咄逼人的巧舌面前溃败了。严峻的纪尧姆太太第一个在女儿的情爱里找到一个理由，让她放弃自己的原则，同意接待德·索默维厄先生——她满心想的是要对他严加盘问一番。
老呢绒商去找约瑟夫·勒巴，把事情的原委告诉了他。六点半，被艺术家画进了不朽之作的那间饭厅里，天窗下齐聚了罗甘先生和罗甘太太、年轻画家和他迷人的奥古斯丁、以耐心为幸福的约瑟夫·勒巴，以及头痛初愈的维尔日妮小姐。纪尧姆先生和太太眼看着一双儿女都有了归宿，猫打球的家业又将回到能干的手里。到了上甜点的时候，泰奥多尔把他们没能去看的那幅神妙的画——画的是老店铺的内景——赠给了两位老人，他们全家的幸福正是拜这幅画所赐，两位老人的满意达到了顶点。
「这画真好看！」纪尧姆喊道，「想想看，竟然有人肯出三万法郎买它！」
「因为画里看得出我的帽带。」纪尧姆太太说。
「还有展开的呢料！」勒巴补了一句，「简直像拿手就能抓起来。」
「呢绒织物总是画得出彩，」画家答道，「我们这些现代艺术家，若能摸着古代呢绒画法的完美的边儿，就是天大的幸福了。」
「原来您喜欢呢绒！」老纪尧姆喊道，「那么，天哪！为这个握握手，我的年轻朋友。既然您敬重买卖，咱们就谈得拢。买卖凭什么让人瞧不起呢？世界就是从买卖开始的，亚当拿乐园换了一只苹果嘛。不过他这笔买卖可不划算！」老人开怀大笑，香槟又给他添了胆，他一杯杯大方地劝人。蒙在年轻艺术家眼睛上的带子那样厚，他竟觉得未来的公婆和蔼可亲。他也不端架子，拣最得体的笑话说了几个，给他们助兴。于是他讨得了每个人的欢心。

===Original===

In the evening, when the drawing-room, furnished with what Madame Guillaume called “everything handsome,” was deserted, and while she flitted from the table to the chimneypiece, from the candelabra to the tall candlesticks, hastily blowing out the wax lights, the worthy draper, who was always clear-sighted when money was in question, called Augustine to him, and seating her on his knee, spoke as follows:﻿—
“My dear child, you shall marry your Sommervieux since you insist; you may, if you like, risk your capital in happiness. But I am not going to be hoodwinked by the thirty thousand francs to be made by spoiling good canvas. Money that is lightly earned is lightly spent. Did I not hear that harebrained youngster declare this evening that money was made round that it might roll. If it is round for spendthrifts, it is flat for saving folks who pile it up. Now, my child, that fine gentleman talks of giving you carriages and diamonds! He has money, let him spend it on you; so be it. It is no concern of mine. But as to what I can give you, I will not have the crown-pieces I have picked up with so much toil wasted in carriages and frippery. Those who spend too fast never grow rich. A hundred thousand crowns, which is your fortune, will not buy up Paris. It is all very well to look forward to a few hundred thousand francs to be yours some day; I shall keep you waiting for them as long as possible, by Gad! So I took your lover aside, and a man who managed the Lecocq bankruptcy had not much difficulty in persuading the artist to marry under a settlement of his wife’s money on herself. I will keep an eye on the marriage contract to see that what he is to settle on you is safely tied up. So now, my child, I hope to be a grandfather, by Gad! I will begin at once to lay up for my grandchildren; but swear to me, here and now, never to sign any papers relating to money without my advice; and if I go soon to join old Father Chevrel, promise to consult young Lebas, your brother-in-law.”
“Yes, father, I swear it.”
At these words, spoken in a gentle voice, the old man kissed his daughter on both cheeks. That night the lovers slept as soundly as Monsieur and Madame Guillaume.
---
Some few months after this memorable Sunday the high altar of Saint-Leu was the scene of two very different weddings.

===Chinese===

晚上，那间陈设着纪尧姆太太所谓「样样气派」的客厅空下来以后，她从桌子飞到壁炉架，从烛台飞到高脚蜡烛架，急急忙忙吹熄蜡烛；这位一涉及钱就眼明心亮的可敬呢绒商把奥古斯丁叫到跟前，让她坐在自己膝上，说了下面这番话：——
「亲爱的孩子，你既然执意要嫁你的索默维厄，就嫁吧；你高兴，就把你的本钱押在幸福上好了。可是我不会让那糟蹋好画布换来的三万法郎迷了心窍。来得容易的钱，去得也容易。今晚我不是听见那个毛头小伙子宣称，钱造得圆圆的，就是为了让它滚吗。在败家子手里它是圆的，在攒钱的节俭人手里，它是扁的、摞起来的。我说孩子，那位漂亮先生许诺给你马车和钻石！他有钱，让他花在你身上好了；由他去。这不关我的事。可我自己能给你的，我不许人把我辛辛苦苦捡来的埃居糟蹋在车马和花哨玩意儿上。花得太快的人永远富不了。十万埃居——那是你的财产——买不下整个巴黎。你尽管指望有朝一日到手几十万法郎好了；可我要叫你尽量多等些年头，天哪！所以我把你那位情人拉到一边，一个办过勒科克破产案的人，要说服一个艺术家接受妻子财产归妻子本人享有的婚姻财产制，并不费什么事。婚约我要亲自过目，看他许给你的那份，拴得牢不牢。就这样，孩子，我盼着抱外孙了，天哪！我马上就动手给外孙们攒钱；可你要当场向我起誓：凡有关钱款的文书，没有我的忠告，永远不许签字；我要是早早去陪谢弗勒尔老爹了，就答应去请教你的姐夫小勒巴。」
「好的，爸爸，我起誓。」
老人用温和的声音说了这番话，末了在女儿的双颊上亲了亲。这一夜，一对恋人睡得同纪尧姆先生和太太一样沉。
---
那个难忘的星期天之后几个月，圣勒乌的主祭坛前举行了两场迥然不同的婚礼。

===Original===

Augustine and Thédore appeared in all the radiance of happiness, their eyes beaming with love, dressed with elegance, while a fine carriage waited for them. Virginie, who had come in a good hired fly with the rest of the family, humbly followed her younger sister, dressed in the simplest fashion like a shadow necessary to the harmony of the picture. Monsieur Guillaume had exerted himself to the utmost in the church to get Virginie married before Augustine, but the priests, high and low, persisted in addressing the more elegant of the two brides. He heard some of his neighbors highly approving the good sense of Mademoiselle Virginie, who was making, as they said, the more substantial match, and remaining faithful to the neighborhood; while they fired a few taunts, prompted by envy of Augustine, who was marrying an artist and a man of rank; adding, with a sort of dismay, that if the Guillaumes were ambitious, there was an end to the business. An old fan-maker having remarked that such a prodigal would soon bring his wife to beggary, father Guillaume prided himself in petto for his prudence in the matter of marriage settlements. In the evening, after a splendid ball, followed by one of those substantial suppers of which the memory is dying out in the present generation, Monsieur and Madame Guillaume remained in a fine house belonging to them in the Rue du Colombier, where the wedding had been held; Monsieur and Madame Lebas returned in their fly to the old home in the Rue Saint-Denis, to steer the good ship Cat and Racket. The artist, intoxicated with happiness, carried off his beloved Augustine, and eagerly lifting her out of their carriage when it reached the Rue des Trois-Frères, led her to an apartment embellished by all the arts.
The fever of passion which possessed Thédore made a year fly over the young couple without a single cloud to dim the blue sky under which they lived. Life did not hang heavy on the lovers’ hands. Thédore lavished on every day inexhaustible fioriture of enjoyment, and he delighted to vary the transports of passion by the soft languor of those hours of repose when souls soar so high that they seem to have forgotten all bodily union.

===Chinese===

奥古斯丁和泰奥多尔满面幸福的光彩，眼中荡漾着爱情，衣着一派雅致，一辆华美的马车正等着他们。维尔日妮同全家一起坐一辆上好的雇用轿式马车来，衣着朴素之至，像画面和谐所必不可少的一道影子，谦卑地跟在妹妹身后。纪尧姆先生在教堂里使尽浑身解数，想让维尔日妮先于奥古斯丁行礼，可是神甫们上上下下都只认两位新人中装束更讲究的那位。他听见几个邻人极力称赞维尔日妮小姐有见识：照他们的说法，她结的是更实惠的亲事，而且没有离开本街区；对奥古斯丁，他们出于嫉妒挖苦了几句——她嫁的是个艺术家，还是个有爵位的人；又带着几分沮丧补一句：纪尧姆家要是存心高攀，这买卖就算完了。有个做扇子的老头说，这样一位挥霍公子早晚要把老婆带到讨饭的地步；纪尧姆老爹心里暗暗得意自己在婚产上头的精明。晚上，一场盛大的舞会之后，又摆下如今这代人记忆中正在消失的那种实实在在的夜宵；席终，纪尧姆先生和太太留在哥伦比埃街一栋属于他们的漂亮宅子里——婚礼就是在那里办的；勒巴先生和太太坐轿式马车回圣但尼街的老家，去掌猫打球这艘好船的舵。艺术家幸福得醉酗酗的，带着他心爱的奥古斯丁走了；马车到了三兄弟街，他急切地把她抱下车，领进一套被种种艺术装点起来的公寓。
泰奥多尔为激情的狂热所支配，一年光阴在这对小夫妻头顶飞过，没有一朵云翳玷暗他们头上的蓝天。日子在恋人手里从不滞重。泰奥多尔每一天都挥洒着享用不尽的花腔，又喜欢在激情的迷醉之后换上休憩时辰的慵倦——那样的时辰里，灵魂翱翔得那样高，仿佛忘却了一切形体的结合。

===Original===

Augustine was too happy for reflection; she floated on an undulating tide of rapture; she thought she could not do enough by abandoning herself to sanctioned and sacred married love; simple and artless, she had no coquetry, no reserves, none of the dominion which a worldly-minded girl acquires over her husband by ingenious caprice; she loved too well to calculate for the future, and never imagined that so exquisite a life could come to an end. Happy in being her husband’s sole delight, she believed that her inextinguishable love would always be her greatest grace in his eyes, as her devotion and obedience would be a perennial charm. And, indeed, the ecstasy of love had made her so brilliantly lovely that her beauty filled her with pride, and gave her confidence that she could always reign over a man so easy to kindle as Monsieur de Sommervieux. Thus her position as a wife brought her no knowledge but the lessons of love.
In the midst of her happiness, she was still the simple child who had lived in obscurity in the Rue Saint-Denis, and who never thought of acquiring the manners, the information, the tone of the world she had to live in. Her words being the words of love, she revealed in them, no doubt, a certain pliancy of mind and a certain refinement of speech; but she used the language common to all women when they find themselves plunged in passion, which seems to be their element. When, by chance, Augustine expressed an idea that did not harmonize with Thédore’s, the young artist laughed, as we laugh at the first mistakes of a foreigner, though they end by annoying us if they are not corrected.
In spite of all this lovemaking, by the end of this year, as delightful as it was swift, Sommervieux felt one morning the need for resuming his work and his old habits. His wife was expecting their first child. He saw some friends again. During the tedious discomforts of the year when a young wife is nursing an infant for the first time, he worked, no doubt, with zeal, but he occasionally sought diversion in the fashionable world. The house which he was best pleased to frequent was that of the Duchesse de Carigliano, who had at last attracted the celebrated artist to her parties.

===Chinese===

奥古斯丁幸福得无暇思索；她漂荡在起伏不定的狂喜的潮水上；她以为把自己交付给名正言顺、神圣的夫妻之爱，怎样做都不为过；她单纯天真，毫无卖弄，毫无保留，也没有那种有心计的姑娘靠巧妙的小性子在与丈夫相处中赚下的统治权；她爱得太深，顾不上为将来盘算，从不曾想过这样精美的生活会有一天终结。以做丈夫唯一的赏心乐事为幸福，她相信自己那不灭的爱永远是他眼中最大的恩宠，正如她的奉献与顺从将是常开的魅力之花。的确，爱的狂喜使她容光焕发，艳丽照人，她的美貌叫她自家骄傲，也让她自信永远能统治德·索默维厄先生这样一个一点就着的人。这样，妻子的身份没有教给她别的，只教给她爱情的功课。
身在幸福之中，她依然是那个在圣但尼街默默长大的单纯的孩子，从没想到要学她将生活在其中的那个世界的举止、见闻和腔调。她开口是爱的言语，里面固然透出几分柔顺的心性和几分谈吐的雅致；但她说的是一切女人沉浸于激情时通用的话——激情仿佛正是她们的天性。偶尔，奥古斯丁表达了一个与泰奥多尔不甚合拍的想法，年轻艺术家便笑起来，像我们笑一个外国人初来的错误；只是那些错误若不改，笑到最后便成了恼。
纵有这许多恩爱，这一年——又甜美又飞快——过到头的时候，一天早晨，索默维厄感到有必要重新拾起他的工作和旧习惯了。妻子怀上了他们的第一个孩子。他又见了些朋友。在年轻妻子头一回哺乳婴儿、诸事烦闷的一年里，他工作无疑还是勤奋的，但偶尔也到交际场中寻些消遣。他去得最称心的，是卡里利亚诺公爵夫人的府上——她终于把这位名画家引到了她的晚会里。

===Original===

When Augustine was quite well again, and her boy no longer required the assiduous care which debars a mother from social pleasures, Thédore had come to the stage of wishing to know the joys of satisfied vanity to be found in society by a man who shows himself with a handsome woman, the object of envy and admiration.
To figure in drawing-rooms with the reflected lustre of her husband’s fame, and to find other women envious of her, was to Augustine a new harvest of pleasures; but it was the last gleam of conjugal happiness. She first wounded her husband’s vanity when, in spite of vain efforts, she betrayed her ignorance, the inelegance of her language, and the narrowness of her ideas. Sommervieux’s nature, subjugated for nearly two years and a half by the first transports of love, now, in the calm of less new possession, recovered its bent and habits, for a while diverted from their channel. Poetry, painting, and the subtle joys of imagination have inalienable rights over a lofty spirit. These cravings of a powerful soul had not been starved in Thédore during these two years; they had only found fresh pasture. As soon as the meadows of love had been ransacked, and the artist had gathered roses and cornflowers as the children do, so greedily that he did not see that his hands could hold no more, the scene changed. When the painter showed his wife the sketches for his finest compositions he heard her exclaim, as her father had done, “How pretty!” This tepid admiration was not the outcome of conscientious feeling, but of her faith on the strength of love.
Augustine cared more for a look than for the finest picture. The only sublime she knew was that of the heart. At last Thédore could not resist the evidence of the cruel fact﻿—his wife was insensible to poetry, she did not dwell in his sphere, she could not follow him in all his vagaries, his inventions, his joys and his sorrows; she walked groveling in the world of reality, while his head was in the skies. Common minds cannot appreciate the perennial sufferings of a being who, while bound to another by the most intimate affections, is obliged constantly to suppress the dearest flights of his soul, and to thrust down into the void those images which a magic power compels him to create.

===Chinese===

待奥古斯丁完全康复，孩子也不再需要那种把母亲拴住、不许她沾社交之乐的贴身照料时，泰奥多尔已到了这样一个阶段：他想知道一个带着美丽太太出入交际场的男人所尝到的虚荣心的满足——她惹人艳羡，惹人仰慕。
凭丈夫声名的光彩在客厅里露脸，看到别的女人嫉妒自己，对奥古斯丁是一茬新的丰收的乐趣；可这也是夫妻幸福的最后一道光了。她头一回伤了丈夫的虚荣心，是在白费力气之后，泄露了自己的无知、言谈的不雅和见识的狭窄。索默维厄的天性，被最初的爱的狂热压制了差不多两年半，如今，在不再那么新鲜的占有的平静里，又恢复了本来的趋向和习惯——它们不过暂时改了道。诗、绘画和想象的微妙乐趣，对一颗高迈的心灵拥有不可剥夺的权利。这颗强健灵魂的这些渴念，两年里在泰奥多尔身上并没有挨饿，只是另辟了牧场。爱情的草场一旦被翻检一空，艺术家也像孩子们那样贪婪地采完了玫瑰和矢车菊，贪婪得看不见手里已经捧不下——场景便换了。当画家把最得意的构图草稿拿给妻子看时，他听见她像她父亲那样喊一声：「真好看！」这温吞吞的赞美并非出于真心实意的感受，而是出于她凭着爱情建立起来的信任。
奥古斯丁把一个眼色看得比最美的画还重。她所知道的唯一的崇高，是心灵的崇高。终于，泰奥多尔抗拒不了那个残酷事实的明证——妻子对诗无动于衷，她不住在他的天地里，她跟不上他全部的奇思、他的创造、他的欢乐与忧伤；她匍匐在现实的世界里走路，而他的头颅高在云端。庸常的心智体会不到那种终身的痛苦：一个人被最亲密的情感与另一个人缚在一起，却不得不时时按住灵魂最宝贵的飞翔，把那股魔法逼他创造出来的种种意象，硬生生按回虚空里去。

===Original===

To him the torture is all the more intolerable because his feeling towards his companion enjoins, as its first law, that they should have no concealments, but mingle the aspirations of their thought as perfectly as the effusions of their soul. The demands of nature are not to be cheated. She is as inexorable as necessity, which is, indeed, a sort of social nature. Sommervieux took refuge in the peace and silence of his studio, hoping that the habit of living with artists might mould his wife and develop in her the dormant germs of lofty intelligence which some superior minds suppose must exist in every being. But Augustine was too sincerely religious not to take fright at the tone of artists. At the first dinner Thédore gave, she heard a young painter say, with the childlike lightness, which to her was unintelligible, and which redeems a jest from the taint of profanity, “But, madame, your Paradise cannot be more beautiful than Raphael’s *Transfiguration*!﻿—Well, and I got tired of looking at that.”
Thus Augustine came among this sparkling set in a spirit of distrust which no one could fail to see. She was a restraint on their freedom. Now an artist who feels restraint is pitiless; he stays away, or laughs it to scorn. Madame Guillaume, among other absurdities, had an excessive notion of the dignity she considered the prerogative of a married woman; and Augustine, though she had often made fun of it, could not help a slight imitation of her mother’s primness. This extreme propriety, which virtuous wives do not always avoid, suggested a few epigrams in the form of sketches, in which the harmless jest was in such good taste that Sommervieux could not take offence; and even if they had been more severe, these pleasantries were after all only reprisals from his friends. Still, nothing could seem a trifle to a spirit so open as Thédore’s to impressions from without. A coldness insensibly crept over him, and inevitably spread. To attain conjugal happiness we must climb a hill whose summit is a narrow ridge, close to a steep and slippery descent: the painter’s love was falling down it.

===Chinese===

对他来说，这刑罚尤其难以忍受，因为他对伴侣的感情，其第一条法则便是不设隐瞒，让两人思想的向往像灵魂的倾吐一样交融无间。天性的要求是骗不过去的。它像必然性一样毫不通融——必然性，说到底，就是一种社会的天性。索默维厄躲进画室的安宁与寂静里，指望与艺术家朝夕相处的习惯能塑造妻子，催发她体内沉睡的高贵心智的种子——有些卓越的心灵认定这种子人皆有之。可是奥古斯丁的宗教信仰太真诚，不能不为艺术家们的腔调受惊。泰奥多尔请的第一顿客饭上，她听见一个年轻画家以孩子般的天真口吻说——那口吻她听不懂，却正使玩笑免除了亵渎的气味——「可是，太太，您的天堂再美，也美不过拉斐尔的《基督显圣容》！——嘿，那张画我都看腻了。」
于是奥古斯丁来到这群妙人中间，满心的不信任，谁都看得出来。她成了他们放浪的拘束。而一个感到拘束的艺术家是无情的：他从此不来，或者一笑置之。纪尧姆太太的诸多荒唐见解里，有一条把已婚妇人的尊严看成她的特权，看得过了头；奥古斯丁虽常常笑话这一点，却忍不住多少学了些母亲的古板。这种贤惠太太也不总能避免的过分端谨，招来了几幅速写式的小讽刺画；那无伤大雅的玩笑品位极高，索默维厄无从动气；就算画得再刻薄些，这些打趣毕竟只是朋友们的报复。然而，对泰奥多尔这样一颗向外部印象敞开的心灵，没有一件事是小节。一层冷淡不知不觉罩上了他，并且不可避免地蔓延开来。要抵达夫妻的幸福，必须登上一座小山，山顶是一道窄脊，旁边便是又陡又滑的下坡：画家的爱正从那坡上往下滚。

===Original===

He regarded his wife as incapable of appreciating the moral considerations which justified him in his own eyes for his singular behavior to her, and believed himself quite innocent in hiding from her thoughts she could not enter into, and peccadilloes outside the jurisdiction of a bourgeois conscience. Augustine wrapped herself in sullen and silent grief. These unconfessed feelings placed a shroud between the husband and wife which could not fail to grow thicker day by day. Though her husband never failed in consideration for her, Augustine could not help trembling as she saw that he kept for the outer world those treasures of wit and grace that he formerly would lay at her feet. She soon began to find sinister meaning in the jocular speeches that are current in the world as to the inconstancy of men. She made no complaints, but her demeanor conveyed reproach.
Three years after her marriage this pretty young woman, who dashed past in her handsome carriage, and lived in a sphere of glory and riches to the envy of heedless folk incapable of taking a just view of the situations of life, was a prey to intense grief. She lost her color; she reflected; she made comparisons; then sorrow unfolded to her the first lessons of experience. She determined to restrict herself bravely within the round of duty, hoping that by this generous conduct she might sooner or later win back her husband’s love. But it was not so. When Sommervieux, fired with work, came in from his studio, Augustine did not put away her work so quickly but that the painter might find his wife mending the household linen, and his own, with all the care of a good housewife. She supplied generously and without a murmur the money needed for his lavishness; but in her anxiety to husband her dear Thédore’s fortune, she was strictly economical for herself and in certain details of domestic management. Such conduct is incompatible with the easygoing habits of artists, who, at the end of their life, have enjoyed it so keenly that they never inquire into the causes of their ruin.
It is useless to note every tint of shadow by which the brilliant hues of their honeymoon were overcast till they were lost in utter blackness.

===Chinese===

他把妻子看作不能领会那些道德考量的人——那些考量使他在自己眼里为他对她的古怪行为开脱了责任；他自以为清白，向她隐瞒她无法参与的思想，隐瞒市民良心管不着的小过失。奥古斯丁裹起了阴郁而沉默的悲伤。这些不曾说破的情绪，在夫妻之间挂起了一层裹尸布，且不能不一天天加厚。丈夫对她的礼数虽然从不短缺，奥古斯丁看见他把机智与风雅的宝藏留给外面的世界——那些他从前要捧到她脚边的宝贝——还是不禁战栗。不久，她便开始从世人那些关于男人薄情的戏言里，听出凶险的意味来。她没有怨言，可她的神色句句是责备。
婚后三年，这位坐着华美马车飞驰而过、活在光荣与富足之中、令那些看不清人生处境的粗心人艳羡不已的漂亮少妇，正被深重的悲伤啃噬。她失去了血色；她思索；她比较；随后，忧愁给她展开了经验的第一课。她决意勇敢地把自己限制在责任的圈子里，指望凭这份慷慨的操行，迟早赢回丈夫的爱。然而并非如此。索默维厄带着工作的火气从画室进来时，奥古斯丁收针线收得不够快，画家便会撞见妻子正以好主妇的细心缝补家用的衬衣——还有他自己的。他挥霍所需的钱，她慷慨供给，毫无怨言；可她一心要守住亲爱的泰奥多尔的财产，对自己、对家务的某些细处便一省再省。这样的行为与艺术家散漫的习性格格不入——艺术家们到一生尽头，享受得太痛快了，从不去追究自己败落的原因。
他们蜜月鲜亮的色彩，如何被一层层暗影罩住，直至没入全黑，一一记下是无用的。

===Original===

One evening poor Augustine, who had for some time heard her husband speak with enthusiasm of the Duchesse de Carigliano, received from a friend certain malignantly charitable warnings as to the nature of the attachment which Sommervieux had formed for this celebrated flirt of the Imperial Court. At one-and-twenty, in all the splendor of youth and beauty, Augustine saw herself deserted for a woman of six-and-thirty. Feeling herself so wretched in the midst of a world of festivity which to her was a blank, the poor little thing could no longer understand the admiration she excited, or the envy of which she was the object. Her face assumed a different expression. Melancholy, tinged her features with the sweetness of resignation and the pallor of scorned love. Ere long she too was courted by the most fascinating men; but she remained lonely and virtuous. Some contemptuous words which escaped her husband filled her with incredible despair. A sinister flash showed her the breaches which, as a result of her sordid education, hindered the perfect union of her soul with Théodore’s; she loved him well enough to absolve him and condemn herself. She shed tears of blood, and perceived, too late, that there are mésalliances of the spirit as well as of rank and habits. As she recalled the early raptures of their union, she understood the full extent of that lost happiness, and accepted the conclusion that so rich a harvest of love was in itself a whole life, which only sorrow could pay for. At the same time, she loved too truly to lose all hope. At one-and-twenty she dared undertake to educate herself, and make her imagination, at least, worthy of that she admired. “If I am not a poet,” thought she, “at any rate, I will understand poetry.”
Then, with all the strength of will, all the energy which every woman can display when she loves, Madame de Sommervieux tried to alter her character, her manners, and her habits; but by dint of devouring books and learning undauntedly, she only succeeded in becoming less ignorant. Lightness of wit and the graces of conversation are a gift of nature, or the fruit of education begun in the cradle. She could appreciate music and enjoy it, but she could not sing with taste. She understood literature and the beauties of poetry, but it was too late to cultivate her refractory memory.

===Chinese===

一天晚上，可怜的奥古斯丁——她早听说丈夫满怀热情地谈论卡里利亚诺公爵夫人——从一个朋友那里接到几番恶意而好心的警告，说索默维厄对帝国宫廷这位出名的风流女子所生的情意究竟是什么性质。二十一岁，正当青春与美貌的盛年，奥古斯丁眼看自己被一个三十六岁的女人比了下去。置身于对她而言只是一片空白的欢庆世界，她自觉那样不幸，这可怜的小东西再也理解不了自己惹起的倾慕、自己招来的嫉妒。她的脸换了一种表情。忧郁用听天由命的甜美和被弃之爱的苍白，染了她的容貌。不久，最有魅力的男人们也来向她献殷勤；可她依旧孤独而贞静。丈夫脱口而出的几句轻蔑话，使她陷入难以置信的绝望。一道凶险的闪光向她照出：由于她所受的鄙俗教育，她的灵魂与泰奥多尔的灵魂之间横着怎样的裂口——那裂口阻碍着两颗灵魂的完美结合；她爱他爱得足以宽恕他、怪罪自己。她流着血泪，太晚地明白：门第与习尚之外，还有心灵的门不当户不对。回想结合之初的狂喜，她掂出了那份逝去的幸福的全部分量，也接受了这样的结论：爱情如此丰盛的一次收获，本身就是整整一生，只有用悲哀来偿付。但同时，她爱得太真，不肯断绝一切希望。二十一岁上，她敢于着手自我教育，至少让自己的想象力配得上她所仰慕的东西。「我做不成诗人，」她想，「至少，我要懂得诗。」
于是，凭着每个恋爱中的女人都拿得出来的全部意志与精力，德·索默维厄太太努力改造自己的性格、举止和习惯；可是书吞了一本又一本，学得毫不气馁，也不过让自己不那么无知而已。心智的轻盈与谈吐的风致，是天赋，或是摇篮里就开始的教养结出的果。她能鉴赏音乐、乐于听乐，却唱不出韵味。她懂得文学和诗的美，但再要雕琢她那倔强的记性，已经太迟。

===Original===

She listened with pleasure to social conversation, but she could contribute nothing brilliant. Her religious notions and homegrown prejudices were antagonistic to the complete emancipation of her intelligence. Finally, a foregone conclusion against her had stolen into Thédore’s mind, and this she could not conquer. The artist would laugh, at those who flattered him about his wife, and his irony had some foundation; he so overawed the pathetic young creature that, in his presence, or alone with him, she trembled. Hampered by her too eager desire to please, her wits and her knowledge vanished in one absorbing feeling. Even her fidelity vexed the unfaithful husband, who seemed to bid her do wrong by stigmatizing her virtue as insensibility. Augustine tried in vain to abdicate her reason, to yield to her husband’s caprices and whims, to devote herself to the selfishness of his vanity. Her sacrifices bore no fruit. Perhaps they had both let the moment slip when souls may meet in comprehension. One day the young wife’s too sensitive heart received one of those blows which so strain the bonds of feeling that they seem to be broken. She withdrew into solitude. But before long a fatal idea suggested to her to seek counsel and comfort in the bosom of her family.
So one morning she made her way towards the grotesque façade of the humble, silent home where she had spent her childhood. She sighed as she looked up at the sash-window, whence one day she had sent her first kiss to him who now shed as much sorrow as glory on her life. Nothing was changed in the cavern, where the drapery business had, however, started on a new life. Augustine’s sister filled her mother’s old place at the desk. The unhappy young woman met her brother-in-law with his pen behind his ear; he hardly listened to her, he was so full of business. The formidable symptoms of stocktaking were visible all round him; he begged her to excuse him. She was received coldly enough by her sister, who owed her a grudge. In fact, Augustine, in her finery, and stepping out of a handsome carriage, had never been to see her but when passing by. The wife of the prudent Lebas, imagining that want of money was the prime cause of this early call, tried to keep up a tone of reserve which more than once made Augustine smile.

===Chinese===

社交场上的谈话她听得有味，却拿不出光彩来应和。她的宗教观念和土生土长的偏见，同她智识的彻底解放格格不入。更糟的是，一个先入为主的成见早已潜入泰奥多尔心里，这是她攻不破的。有人恭维他的妻子，艺术家便报以讥笑，他的讥讽并非全无根据；他把这可怜的少妇慑服到这步田地：当着他的面，或与他单独相处，她就发抖。一心想讨他欢喜的心思太切，反而缚住了她，她的机敏和学问在一团郁结的情感里消失无踪。连她的忠贞也惹得不忠的丈夫不痛快，他指斥她的美德是无情，仿佛存心擸掇她学坏。奥古斯丁徒劳地想放弃自己的理性，想顺从丈夫的反复无常，想把自己献给他的虚荣的自私。她的牺牲没有结出果实。或许，两颗灵魂本可能相通的那一瞬，早已被他们双双放过。有一天，年轻妻子过分敏感的心挨了一记重击——那类重击绷得感情的纽带似乎就要断了。她躲进了孤独。可不久，一个致命的念头提醒她，去娘家的怀抱里讨主意、寻安慰。
于是一天早晨，她朝那座古怪门面的、谦卑而沉默的宅子走去——她在那里度过了童年。她抬头望了望那扇吊窗，叹了口气：有一天，她就是从那扇窗里，把第一个吻送给了那个如今给她的人生洒下多少悲哀、也洒下多少光荣的人。洞穴里什么也没有变，只是呢绒生意翻开了新的一页。奥古斯丁的姐姐坐在账台后母亲当年的位子上。不幸的少妇碰见姐夫，他耳朵上夹着笔；他满脑子生意，几乎没有听她说话。盘货的大阵仗在他四周历历在目；他求她恕不奉陪。姐姐接待她相当冷淡——姐姐对她怀恨在心。原来，奥古斯丁一身盛装，从漂亮的马车上下来，从前只是路过时才来看看她。谨慎的勒巴的太太，以为手头缺钱是妹妹这么早登门的主因，便端出一副矜持的口吻，那口吻不止一次惹得奥古斯丁想笑。

===Original===

The painter’s wife perceived that, apart from the cap and lappets, her mother had found in Virginie a successor who could uphold the ancient honor of the Cat and Racket. At breakfast she observed certain changes in the management of the house which did honor to Lebas’ good sense; the assistants did not rise before dessert; they were allowed to talk, and the abundant meal spoke of ease without luxury. The fashionable woman found some tickets for a box at the Français, where she remembered having seen her sister from time to time. Madame Lebas had a cashmere shawl over her shoulders, of which the value bore witness to her husband’s generosity to her. In short, the couple were keeping pace with the times. During the two-thirds of the day she spent there, Augustine was touched to the heart by the equable happiness, devoid, to be sure, of all emotion, but equally free from storms, enjoyed by this well-matched couple. They had accepted life as a commercial enterprise, in which, above all, they must do credit to the business. Not finding any great love in her husband, Virginie had set to work to create it. Having by degrees learned to esteem and care for his wife, the time that his happiness had taken to germinate was to Joseph Lebas a guarantee of its durability. Hence, when Augustine plaintively set forth her painful position, she had to face the deluge of commonplace morality which the traditions of the Rue Saint-Denis furnished to her sister.
“The mischief is done, wife,” said Joseph Lebas; “we must try to give our sister good advice.” Then the clever tradesman ponderously analyzed the resources which law and custom might offer Augustine as a means of escape at this crisis; he ticketed every argument, so to speak, and arranged them in their degrees of weight under various categories, as though they were articles of merchandise of different qualities; then he put them in the scale, weighed them, and ended by showing the necessity for his sister-in-law’s taking violent steps which could not satisfy the love she still had for her husband; and, indeed, the feeling had revived in all its strength when she heard Joseph Lebas speak of legal proceedings. Augustine thanked them, and returned home even more undecided than she had been before consulting them.

===Chinese===

画家的妻子看出，撇开软帽和帽带不算，母亲在维尔日妮身上找到了一个能撑起猫打球古老门风的继承人。早餐时，她注意到持家方面的几处变化，为勒巴的见识增光：上甜点之前，伙计们不必起立了；准许他们说话了；丰盛的饭食说的是宽裕，而非奢华。这位时髦女子警见几张法兰西剧院包厢的票——她记得从前时常在那里见到姐姐。勒巴太太肩上披着一条开司米披肩，那价值足见丈夫对她的慷慨。总之，这对夫妻是跟着时代走的。她在那里消磨了大半天，这桩门当户对的婚姻里那种平稳的幸福——固然毫无激荡，却也绝无风波——深深触动了奥古斯丁的心。他们把人生当作一桩买卖来经营，头一条便是不能辱没了商号的信誉。丈夫身上寻不出伟大的爱情，维尔日妮便着手自己创造一个。勒巴渐渐学会敬重和疼爱妻子；这份幸福发芽所费的时间，在约瑟夫·勒巴看来，正是它持久的保证。于是，当奥古斯丁凄凄切切诉说自己痛苦的处境时，她迎面撞上的，是圣但尼街的传统供给她姐姐的一场平庸道德的倾盆大雨。
「祸事已经出了，老婆子，」约瑟夫·勒巴说，「咱们得想法子给妹子出个好主意。」于是这位精明的商人沉甸甸地剖析起法律与习俗在这场危机中能给奥古斯丁提供哪些脱身之途；可以说，他给每条理由都挂上了签，按分量分门别类码好，仿佛它们是不同成色的商品；然后把它们放上秤，称过分量，末了证明：他的小姨子非采取激烈手段不可，而那样的手段，又断然满足不了她对丈夫余情未了的爱。的确，一听约瑟夫·勒巴谈起诉讼，那份情感又以全部的力气活了过来。奥古斯丁谢过他们，回家时比来请教之前更加没了主意。

===Original===

She now ventured to go to the house in the Rue du Colombier, intending to confide her troubles to her father and mother; for she was like a sick man who, in his desperate plight, tries every prescription, and even puts faith in old wives’ remedies.
The old people received their daughter with an effusiveness that touched her deeply. Her visit brought them some little change, and that to them was worth a fortune. For the last four years they had gone their way like navigators without a goal or a compass. Sitting by the chimney corner, they would talk over their disasters under the old law of *maximum*, of their great investments in cloth, of the way they had weathered bankruptcies, and, above all, the famous failure of Lecocq, Monsieur Guillaume’s battle of Marengo. Then, when they had exhausted the tale of lawsuits, they recapitulated the sum total of their most profitable stocktakings, and told each other old stories of the Saint-Denis quarter. At two o’clock old Guillaume went to cast an eye on the business at the Cat and Racket; on his way back he called at all the shops, formerly the rivals of his own, where the young proprietors hoped to inveigle the old draper into some risky discount, which, as was his wont, he never refused point-blank. Two good Normandy horses were dying of their own fat in the stables of the big house; Madame Guillaume never used them but to drag her on Sundays to high Mass at the parish church. Three times a week the worthy couple kept open house. By the influence of his son-in-law Sommervieux, Monsieur Guillaume had been named a member of the consulting board for the clothing of the Army. Since her husband had stood so high in office, Madame Guillaume had decided that she must receive; her rooms were so crammed with gold and silver ornaments, and furniture, tasteless but of undoubted value, that the simplest room in the house looked like a chapel. Economy and expense seemed to be struggling for the upper hand in every accessory. It was as though Monsieur Guillaume had looked to a good investment, even in the purchase of a candlestick.

===Chinese===

如今她壮着胆子去了哥伦比埃街父母的宅子，打算把苦水向父亲母亲倾吐；她像一个绝境中的病人，什么方子都要试一试，连老太婆的偏方也信。
两位老人接待女儿的那份热络，深深感动了她。她这一来给他们的小日子添了点变化，在他们看来就值一笔家财。四年来，他们像没有目标、没有罗盘的航海人一样过活。坐在壁炉角上，他们把旧日最高限价法下的种种灾难、呢料上的大笔投入、闯过一次次破产的经历，尤其是勒科克那场著名的倒闭——纪尧姆先生的马伦哥战役——翻来覆去地谈。官司谈尽了，就历数他们盈利最丰的几次盘货的总数，再把圣但尼街区的老故事讲给彼此听。两点钟，老纪尧姆去猫打球看看生意；回来路上，家家铺子都进去坐坐——都是从前的同行冤家——年轻的老板们都指望把老呢绒商诱进什么带风险的贴现里，而他也照例从不一口回绝。两匹诺曼底（Normandy）好马在大宅的马厩里活活胖死；纪尧姆太太用它们，不过是星期天拖她去本区教堂望大弥撒。这对可敬的夫妇每星期敞开三次家门。靠着女婿索默维厄的势力，纪尧姆先生被任命为陆军军服咨询委员会的委员。丈夫的官位这样高，纪尧姆太太便认定自己不能不接待宾客了；她的房间里塞满了金银器和家具——毫无品位，却价值确凿——弄得家里最简朴的一间屋子也像座小教堂。节俭和排场仿佛在每一件摆设上争着占上风。仿佛纪尧姆先生连买一只烛台，也指望它是一笔划算的投资。

===Original===

In the midst of this bazaar, where splendor revealed the owner’s want of occupation, Sommervieux’s famous picture filled the place of honor, and in it Monsieur and Madame Guillaume found their chief consolation, turning their eyes, harnessed with eyeglasses, twenty times a day on this presentment of their past life, to them so active and amusing. The appearance of this mansion and these rooms, where everything had an aroma of staleness and mediocrity, the spectacle offered by these two beings, cast away, as it were, on a rock far from the world and the ideas which are life, startled Augustine; she could here contemplate the sequel of the scene of which the first part had struck her at the house of Lebas﻿—a life of stir without movement, a mechanical and instinctive existence like that of the beaver; and then she felt an indefinable pride in her troubles, as she reflected that they had their source in eighteen months of such happiness as, in her eyes, was worth a thousand lives like this; its vacuity seemed to her horrible. However, she concealed this not very charitable feeling, and displayed for her parents her newly-acquired accomplishments of mind, and the ingratiating tenderness that love had revealed to her, disposing them to listen to her matrimonial grievances. Old people have a weakness for this kind of confidence. Madame Guillaume wanted to know the most trivial details of that alien life, which to her seemed almost fabulous. The travels of Baron da la Houtan, which she began again and again and never finished, told her nothing more unheard-of concerning the Canadian savages.
“What, child, your husband shuts himself into a room with naked women! And you are so simple as to believe that he draws them?”
As she uttered this exclamation, the grandmother laid her spectacles on a little worktable, shook her skirts, and clasped her hands on her knees, raised by a foot-warmer, her favorite pedestal.
“But, mother, all artists are obliged to have models.”
“He took good care not to tell us that when he asked leave to marry you. If I had known it, I would never had given my daughter to a man who followed such a trade. Religion forbids such horrors; they are immoral. And at what time of night do you say he comes home?”
“At one o’clock﻿—two﻿—”
The old folks looked at each other in utter amazement.
“Then he gambles?” said Monsieur Guillaume.

===Chinese===

在这座豪华得暴露出主人无所事事的集市中央，索默维厄那幅名画占着荣誉的位置；纪尧姆先生和太太的主要安慰便在其中——他们那双架着眼镜的眼睛，一天二十次转向这幅他们往日生活的写照，那段生活在他们看来是那样忙碌、那样有趣。这座公馆和这些房间的气象——一切都散发着一股陈腐与平庸的气味——这两个人的光景，仿佛流落在一座远离人世、远离那些构成生命的思想的礁石上，让奥古斯丁吃了一惊；她在这里看到的是她在勒巴家初见的那一幕的下文——一场没有动作的奔忙，一种河狸式的机械本能的生存；随即，她对自己的苦难生出一股说不出的骄傲：她想，这苦难源出于十八个月那样一种幸福，在她眼里，那种幸福抵得上一千个这样的生命；这样的日子的空虚，在她看来委实可怕。不过她藏起了这不太厚道的念头，向父母展示了新近修养出来的心智才华，和爱情教给她的那讨人喜欢的温柔，让两老愿意听她诉婚姻的委屈。老年人最爱听这一类体己话。纪尧姆太太想打听那个陌生生活里最琐碎的细节，在她看来那生活几乎近于传奇。德·拉·于唐男爵的游记，她一遍遍从头读起、从未读完，也没告诉过她任何关于加拿大野人的更奇闻的事。
「什么，孩子，你丈夫关在屋里跟光身子的女人待在一起！你就这么傻，信他是画画？」
外婆说出这句惊叹，把眼镜搁在一张小针线桌上，抖了抖裙子，双手扣在膝上——那膝盖搁在她最心爱的台座、一只脚炉上。
「可是，妈，艺术家都得用模特儿。」
「他来求亲的时候，可小心着不告诉我们这一层呢。早知道，我绝不把女儿给一个干这行的男人。宗教禁止这种丑事；这是不道德的。你说他夜里几点回家？」
「一点钟——有时候两点——」
两位老人面面相觑，惊愕不已。
「那么他是在赌钱了？」纪尧姆先生说。

===Original===

“In my day only gamblers stayed out so late.”
Augustine made a face that scorned the accusation.
“He must keep you up through dreadful nights waiting for him,” said Madame Guillaume. “But you go to bed, don’t you? And when he has lost, the wretch wakes you.”
“No, mamma, on the contrary, he is sometimes in very good spirits. Not unfrequently, indeed, when it is fine, he suggests that I should get up and go into the woods.”
“The woods! At that hour? Then have you such a small set of rooms that his bedroom and his sitting-room are not enough, and that he must run about? But it is just to give you cold that the wretch proposes such expeditions. He wants to get rid of you. Did one ever hear of a man settled in life, a well-behaved, quiet man galloping about like a warlock?”
“But, my dear mother, you do not understand that he must have excitement to fire his genius. He is fond of scenes which﻿—”
“I would make scenes for him, fine scenes!” cried Madame Guillaume, interrupting her daughter. “How can you show any consideration to such a man? In the first place, I don’t like his drinking water only; it is not wholesome. Why does he object to see a woman eating? What queer notion is that! But he is mad. All you tell us about him is impossible. A man cannot leave his home without a word, and never come back for ten days. And then he tells you he has been to Dieppe to paint the sea. As if anyone painted the sea! He crams you with a pack of tales that are too absurd.”
Augustine opened her lips to defend her husband; but Madame Guillaume enjoined silence with a wave of her hand, which she obeyed by a survival of habit, and her mother went on in harsh tones: “Don’t talk to me about the man! He never set foot in church excepting to see you and to be married. People without religion are capable of anything. Did Guillaume ever dream of hiding anything from me, of spending three days without saying a word to me, and of chattering afterwards like a blind magpie?”
“My dear mother, you judge superior people too severely. If their ideas were the same as other folks’, they would not be men of genius.”
“Very well, then let men of genius stop at home and not get married. What! A man of genius is to make his wife miserable? And because he is a genius it is all right! Genius, genius!

「我年轻那会儿，只有赌棍才在外面待到那么晚。」
奥古斯丁做了个不屑分辩的鬼脸。
「等你等他，他准让你熬了些可怕的夜，」纪尧姆太太说，「可你是先睡下的，对不对？等他输了钱，那坏蛋就把你叫醒。」
「不，妈妈，正相反，他有时候兴致好得很。天气好的时候，他倒常常撺掇我起床，到树林里去呢。」
「树林！那个钟点？这么说，你们的屋子小得连卧室带客厅都不够他待，非得到处乱跑？那坏蛋拉你出去，就是要让你着凉。他是想甩开你。谁听说过一个成了家的人、一个安分规矩的男人，像个巫师似的骑马狂奔？」
「可是，好妈妈，您不明白，他必须有刺激来点燃他的天才。他喜欢那种场面——」
「我倒要给他些场面，好好的场面！」纪尧姆太太打断女儿喊道，「对这样的男人，你怎么还处处将就？头一条，我不喜欢他只喝水；那不养生。他凭什么见不得女人吃东西？这是什么怪念头！他简直是疯子。你说的他这些事，样样都不像话。一个大男人，一声不吭就离家出走，一走十天不回来。回头还跟你说他上迪耶普画海去了。仿佛有人画海似的！他拿一筐荒唐透顶的鬼话填你。」
奥古斯丁张口要为丈夫辩护；纪尧姆太太一摆手喝住她，她出于积习竟顺从了；母亲又用严厉的口吻说下去：「别跟我提这个人！他进教堂统共两回，一回是看上你，一回是成亲。没有宗教的人什么事都干得出来。纪尧姆几时想过瞒我什么事，几时想过三天不跟我说一句话、过后又像只瞎喜鹊那样聒噪个没完？」
「好妈妈，您把出色的人看得太苛刻了。要是他们的想法同旁人一样，也就不成其为天才了。」
「很好，那就叫天才们待在家里，别结婚。什么！天才就可以叫老婆受罪？因为他是天才，就都对了！天才，天才！

It is not so very clever to say black one minute and white the next, as he does, to interrupt other people, to dance such rigs at home, never to let you know which foot you are to stand on, to compel his wife never to be amused unless my lord is in gay spirits, and to be dull when he is dull.”
“But, mother, the very nature of such imaginations﻿—”
“What are such ‘imaginations’?” Madame Guillaume went on, interrupting her daughter again. “Fine ones his are, my word! What possesses a man that all on a sudden, without consulting a doctor, he takes it into his head to eat nothing but vegetables? If indeed it were from religious motives, it might do him some good﻿—but he has no more religion than a Huguenot. Was there ever a man known who, like him, loved horses better than his fellow-creatures, had his hair curled like a heathen, laid statues under muslin coverlets, shut his shutters in broad day to work by lamplight? There, get along; if he were not so grossly immoral, he would be fit to shut up in a lunatic asylum. Consult Monsieur Loraux, the priest at Saint Sulpice, ask his opinion about it all, and he will tell you that your husband does not behave like a Christian.”
“Oh, mother, can you believe﻿—?”
“Yes, I do believe. You loved him, and you can see none of these things. But I can remember in the early days after your marriage. I met him in the Champs-Élysées. He was on horseback. Well, at one minute he was galloping as hard as he could tear, and then pulled up to a walk. I said to myself at that moment, ‘There is a man devoid of judgment.’ ”
“Ah, ha!” cried Monsieur Guillaume, “how wise I was to have your money settled on yourself with such a queer fellow for a husband!”
When Augustine was so imprudent as to set forth her serious grievances against her husband, the two old people were speechless with indignation. But the word “divorce” was ere long spoken by Madame Guillaume. At the sound of the word divorce the apathetic old draper seemed to wake up. Prompted by his love for his daughter, and also by the excitement which the proceedings would bring into his uneventful life, father Guillaume took up the matter. He made himself the leader of the application for a divorce, laid down the lines of it, almost argued the case; he offered to be at all the charges, to see the lawyers, the pleaders, the judges, to move heaven and earth.

===Chinese===

像他那样，一会儿说黑一会儿说白，抢别人的话头，在家里折腾出那些花样，永远不让你知道该站哪只脚，逼得太太老爷不高兴就不得开心、老爷一沉闷就得跟着沉闷——这算不得多高明！」
「可是，妈妈，这样的想象力，天性本来——」
「什么『想象力』？」纪尧姆太太又打断女儿，「他的那些想象力可真了不得，我的天！一个人中了什么邪，不请教医生，忽然心血来潮只吃素？倘若真是出于宗教的动机，倒也于他有好处——可他的宗教还赶不上一个胡格诺教徒。谁听说过这样的人：像他一样爱马胜过爱同类，头发烫得像个异教徒，给雕像盖上细纱被，大白天天着百叶窗点灯画画？得得得；他要不是伤风败俗到这个地步，倒可以送进疯人院关起来了。去请教圣絮尔皮斯教堂的洛罗神甫，听听他对这一切怎么说，他会告诉你，你丈夫的做派不像个基督徒。」
「哦，妈妈，您怎么能信——？」
「我当然信。你爱他，这些你就都看不见了。可我还记得你出嫁后头些日子的事。我在爱丽舍田园大道碰见他。他骑着马。好嘛，前一刻还没命地飞奔，转眼就勒住马慢步走起来。我当时心里就说：『这人没有定性。』」
「啊哈！」纪尧姆先生喊道，「给女儿挑了这么个怪物做丈夫，我把财产判给你本人，多英明！」
等到奥古斯丁不慎说出对丈夫的严重控诉，两位老人气得说不出话来。可「离婚」这个词不久就从纪尧姆太太嘴里吐了出来。一听「离婚」二字，那麻木的老呢绒商仿佛醒了。出于对女儿的爱，也出于这桩官司给他平淡的日子将带来的刺激，纪尧姆老爹把事情接了过去。他自任离婚申请的主帅，定下方略，几乎亲自起草诉状；他愿意承担全部费用，去见律师、讼师、法官，翻天覆地也要办成。

===Original===

Madame de Sommervieux was frightened, she refused her father’s services, said she would not be separated from her husband even if she were ten times as unhappy, and talked no more about her sorrows. After being overwhelmed by her parents with all the little wordless and consoling kindnesses by which the old couple tried in vain to make up to her for her distress of heart, Augustine went away, feeling the impossibility of making a superior mind intelligible to weak intellects. She had learned that a wife must hide from everyone, even from her parents, woes for which it is so difficult to find sympathy. The storms and sufferings of the upper spheres are appreciated only by the lofty spirits who inhabit there. In any circumstance we can only be judged by our equals.
Thus poor Augustine found herself thrown back on the horror of her meditations, in the cold atmosphere of her home. Study was indifferent to her, since study had not brought her back her husband’s heart. Initiated into the secret of these souls of fire, but bereft of their resources, she was compelled to share their sorrows without sharing their pleasures. She was disgusted with the world, which to her seemed mean and small as compared with the incidents of passion. In short, her life was a failure.
One evening an idea flashed upon her that lighted up her dark grief like a beam from heaven. Such an idea could never have smiled on a heart less pure, less virtuous than hers. She determined to go to the Duchesse de Carigliano, not to ask her to give her back her husband’s heart, but to learn the arts by which it had been captured; to engage the interest of this haughty fine lady for the mother of her lover’s children; to appeal to her and make her the instrument of her future happiness, since she was the cause of her present wretchedness.
So one day Augustine, timid as she was, but armed with supernatural courage, got into her carriage at two in the afternoon to try for admittance to the boudoir of the famous coquette, who was never visible till that hour. Madame de Sommervieux had not yet seen any of the ancient and magnificent mansions of the Faubourg Saint-Germain.

===Chinese===

德·索默维厄太太吓坏了，谢绝了父亲效力，说她哪怕不幸十倍，也不愿离开丈夫，从此不再提自己的伤心事。两位老人把种种无言的、安慰人的小殷勤堆到她身上，想以此补上她心头的亏空，却是徒劳；受宠若惊之后，奥古斯丁走了，心里明白：要让孱弱的头脑懂得一颗高迈的心灵，是不可能的。她学到了一课：做妻子的苦楚，必须对所有人隐瞒，连父母也不例外——那苦楚太难觅得同情。上层的风暴与苦难，唯有栖身那里的高洁灵魂才掂得出分量。无论何种处境，我们只能受同侪的评判。
就这样，可怜的奥古斯丁被抛回她冥想的恐怖之中，抛回家里冷冰冰的空气里。读书引不起她的兴致，因为读书没有换回丈夫的心。她被领进了那些火之灵魂的秘密，却得不到它们的资源，只好分担它们的悲哀，而无缘分享它们的欢乐。她厌恶了交际场——比起激情的种种遭际，那世界在她眼里显得何等卑微、何等狭小。总之，她的一生是失败了。
一天晚上，一个念头闪过她的脑际，像天上来的一道光照亮了她黑色的哀愁。这念头，换一颗不如她纯洁、不如她贞洁的心，是绝不会想到的。她决意去见卡里利亚诺公爵夫人：不是求她归还丈夫的心，而是去学那颗心是怎样被俘获的技艺；去为情人的孩子们的母亲，求得这位高傲贵妇的关切；去恳求她，把她变作自己未来幸福的工具——既然她正是自己眼前不幸的根由。
于是一天，奥古斯丁虽然胆怯，却有超自然的勇气武装着，下午两点登上了马车，去求见那位名声在外的风流美人的闺房——不到这个钟点，那位夫人是从不见客的。圣日耳曼区（Faubourg Saint-Germain）那些古老而壮丽的公馆，德·索默维厄太太还一所都没有见识过。

===Original===

As she made her way through the stately corridors, the handsome staircases, the vast drawing-rooms﻿—full of flowers, though it was in the depth of winter, and decorated with the taste peculiar to women born to opulence or to the elegant habits of the aristocracy, Augustine felt a terrible clutch at her heart; she coveted the secrets of an elegance of which she had never had an idea; she breathed in an air of grandeur which explained the attraction of the house for her husband. When she reached the private rooms of the Duchess she was filled with jealousy and a sort of despair, as she admired the luxurious arrangement of the furniture, the draperies and the hangings. Here disorder was a grace, here luxury affected a certain contempt of splendor. The fragrance that floated in the warm air flattered the sense of smell without offending it. The accessories of the rooms were in harmony with a view, through plate-glass windows, of the lawns in a garden planted with evergreen trees. It was all bewitching, and the art of it was not perceptible. The whole spirit of the mistress of these rooms pervaded the drawing-room where Augustine awaited her. She tried to divine her rival’s character from the aspect of the scattered objects; but there was here something as impenetrable in the disorder as in the symmetry, and to the simple-minded young wife all was a sealed letter. All that she could discern was that, as a woman, the Duchess was a superior person. Then a painful thought came over her.
“Alas! And is it true,” she wondered, “that a simple and loving heart is not all-sufficient to an artist; that to balance the weight of these powerful souls they need a union with feminine souls of a strength equal to their own? If I had been brought up like this siren, our weapons at least might have been equal in the hour of struggle.”
“But I am not at home!” The sharp, harsh words, though spoken in an undertone in the adjoining boudoir, were heard by Augustine, and her heart beat violently.
“The lady is in there,” replied the maid.
“You are an idiot! Show her in,” replied the Duchess, whose voice was sweeter, and had assumed the dulcet tones of politeness. She evidently now meant to be heard.
Augustine shyly entered the room.

她穿行在气派的走廊、华美的楼梯、宽阔的客厅之间——虽是隆冬，客厅里却满是鲜花，装点着唯有生来富贵或惯于贵族优雅的女子才有的趣味——奥古斯丁感到心口被狠狠攥了一把；她艳羡那种她从未想象过的优雅的秘密；她呼吸到一种宏大的空气，它解释了这座宅子对她丈夫的吸引力。到了公爵夫人的私室，她满怀嫉妒和一种绝望，赞叹着家具、帷幔和挂毯的奢华布置。这里，凌乱是一种风致；这里，豪华偏偏摆出一副对豪奢的轻蔑。暖气里浮动的芬芳，讨好着嗅觉而不冒犯它。房间的种种陈设，与平板玻璃窗外一座四季常青的花园里的草坪遥相呼应。一切都迷人，而其匠心却无从察觉。这些房间女主人的整个精神，弥漫在奥古斯丁等候她的客厅里。她想从散置的物件上占出情敌的性情；可这里的凌乱同这里的对称一样深不可测，对心地单纯的少妇来说，一切都是一封拆不开的信。她所能看出的只有一点：作为女人，公爵夫人是个非凡的人物。这时，一个痛楚的念头袭上她的心头。
「唉！难道这是真的，」她想，「对一位艺术家，一颗单纯而痴情的心并不是一切；这些强有力的灵魂，要有与她们自身力量相当的女子灵魂与之为偶，才压得住秤？倘若我从小也像这位妖姬这样调教，至少搏杀的时刻，我们的武器还算旗鼓相当。」
「可我谁也不见！」尖利刺耳的话虽是压低了声音在隔壁闺房里说的，奥古斯丁却听见了，心猛跳起来。
「夫人在里面等着呢。」女仆答道。
「你是个蠢货！请她进来。」公爵夫人答话了，声音甜了下去，换上了客套的柔腔。她这回显然是有意让人听见的。
奥古斯丁怯生生地进了屋。

===Original===

At the end of the dainty boudoir she saw the Duchess lounging luxuriously on an ottoman covered with brown velvet and placed in the centre of a sort of apse outlined by soft folds of white muslin over a yellow lining. Ornaments of gilt bronze, arranged with exquisite taste, enhanced this sort of dais, under which the Duchess reclined like a Greek statue. The dark hue of the velvet gave relief to every fascinating charm. A subdued light, friendly to her beauty, fell like a reflection rather than a direct illumination. A few rare flowers raised their perfumed heads from costly Sèvres vases. At the moment when this picture was presented to Augustine’s astonished eyes, she was approaching so noiselessly that she caught a glance from those of the enchantress. This look seemed to say to someone whom Augustine did not at first perceive, “Stay; you will see a pretty woman, and make her visit seem less of a bore.”
On seeing Augustine, the Duchess rose and made her sit down by her.
“And to what do I owe the pleasure of this visit, madame?” she said with a most gracious smile.
“Why all the falseness?” thought Augustine, replying only with a bow.
Her silence was compulsory. The young woman saw before her a superfluous witness of the scene. This personage was, of all the Colonels in the army, the youngest, the most fashionable, and the finest man. His face, full of life and youth, but already expressive, was further enhanced by a small moustache twirled up into points, and as black as jet, by a full imperial, by whiskers carefully combed, and a forest of black hair in some disorder. He was whisking a riding whip with an air of ease and freedom which suited his self-satisfied expression and the elegance of his dress; the ribbons attached to his buttonhole were carelessly tied, and he seemed to pride himself much more on his smart appearance than on his courage. Augustine looked at the Duchesse de Carigliano, and indicated the Colonel by a sidelong glance. All its mute appeal was understood.
“Goodbye, then, Monsieur d’Aiglemont, we shall meet in the Bois de Boulogne.”
These words were spoken by the siren as though they were the result of an agreement made before Augustine’s arrival, and she winged them with a threatening look that the officer deserved perhaps for the admiration he showed in gazing at the modest flower, which contrasted so well with the haughty Duchess.

在雅致的闺房尽头，她看见公爵夫人慵懒地歪在一张蒙棕色丝绒的躺榻上；躺榻安置在一个半圆凹龛似的所在正中，黄衬底上垂着一道道白细纱的软褶。镀金青铜的饰物以极精的趣味点缀着这座矮坛，公爵夫人斜倚其下，宛如一尊希腊雕像。丝绒的深色把每一处诱人的魅力都衬托出来。一道柔光垂怜着她的美貌，与其说直接照亮，不如说是一抹反光。几枝名贵花卉从贵重的塞夫勒瓷瓶里探出芬芳的头。这幅图景映入奥古斯丁惊异的眼睛时，她走得那样轻，正好接住妖姬投来的一瞥。那一瞥仿佛是对某个奥古斯丁起初没有察觉的人说的：「留下吧；你能见到一个漂亮女人，她这趟来访也不那么无聊了。」
一见到奥古斯丁，公爵夫人便起身让她在自己身边坐下。
「夫人是哪阵好风给吹来的？」她带着一团和气的笑容说。
「何必这样假惺惺！」奥古斯丁心里想，只屈膝还了一礼。
她的沉默是迫不得已。少妇看见眼前多了一位这一幕的多余看客。这位人物，在全军的上校里，最年轻、最时髦、身段最漂亮。他的脸满是生气与青春，却已很有气概，再加上两撇捻得尖尖的、乌黑如漆的小胡子、一部络腮胡、梳理得整整齐齐的颊须，和一头微乱的浓密黑发，越发精神。他潇洒自在地甩着一根马鞭，那副神情正合他志得意满的表情和一身考究的装束；纽扣眼上系的勋带随随便便打着结；他引以为豪的，看去更多是他的漂亮仪表，而非他的胆气。奥古斯丁望了望卡里利亚诺公爵夫人，用眼角指了指上校。这一记无声的恳求全被领会了。
「那么再会，德·艾格勒蒙先生，咱们布洛涅树林见。」
妖姬说这几句话的口气，仿佛它们是奥古斯丁到来之前就讲定的一般；话上还添了一记威吓的眼色——军官挨这一记或许不冤：他方才凝望这朵朴素的花时那份倾慕，与高傲的公爵夫人一比，未免太扎眼了。

The young fop bowed in silence, turned on the heels of his boots, and gracefully quitted the boudoir. At this instant, Augustine, watching her rival, whose eyes seemed to follow the brilliant officer, detected in that glance a sentiment of which the transient expression is known to every woman. She perceived with the deepest anguish that her visit would be useless; this lady, full of artifice, was too greedy of homage not to have a ruthless heart.
“Madame,” said Augustine in a broken voice, “the step I am about to take will seem to you very strange; but there is a madness of despair which ought to excuse anything. I understand only too well why Thédore prefers your house to any other, and why your mind has so much power over his. Alas! I have only to look into myself to find more than ample reasons. But I am devoted to my husband, madame. Two years of tears have not effaced his image from my heart, though I have lost his. In my folly I dared to dream of a contest with you; and I have come to you to ask you by what means I may triumph over yourself. Oh, madame,” cried the young wife, ardently seizing the hand which her rival allowed her to hold, “I will never pray to God for my own happiness with so much fervor as I will beseech Him for yours, if you will help me to win back Sommervieux’s regard﻿—I will not say his love. I have no hope but in you. Ah! tell me how you could please him, and make him forget the first days﻿—” At these words Augustine broke down, suffocated with sobs she could not suppress. Ashamed of her weakness, she hid her face in her handkerchief, which she bathed with tears.
“What a child you are, my dear little beauty!” said the Duchess, carried away by the novelty of such a scene, and touched, in spite of herself, at receiving such homage from the most perfect virtue perhaps in Paris. She took the young wife’s handkerchief, and herself wiped the tears from her eyes, soothing her by a few monosyllables murmured with gracious compassion. After a moment’s silence the Duchess, grasping poor Augustine’s hands in both her own﻿—hands that had a rare character of dignity and powerful beauty﻿—said in a gentle and friendly voice: “My first warning is to advise you not to weep so bitterly; tears are disfiguring. We must learn to deal firmly with the sorrows that make us ill, for love does not linger long by a sickbed.
