## La Grenadière / 石榴居
===Original===

To D. W.
La Grenadière is a little house on the right bank of the Loire as you go down stream, about a mile below the bridge of Tours. At this point the river, broad as a lake, and covered with scattered green islands, flows between two lines of cliff, where country houses built uniformly of white stone stand among their gardens and vineyards. The finest fruit in the world ripens there with a southern exposure. The patient toil of many generations has cut terraces in the cliff, so that the face of the rock reflects the rays of the sun, and the produce of hot climates may be grown out of doors in an artificially high temperature.
---
A church spire, rising out of one of the shallower dips in the line of cliffs, marks the little village of Saint-Cyr, to which the scattered houses all belong. And yet a little further the Choisille flows into the Loire, through a fertile valley cut in the long low downs.
La Grenadière itself, halfway up the hillside, and about a hundred paces from the church, is one of those old-fashioned houses dating back some two or three hundred years, which you find in every picturesque spot in Touraine. A fissure in the rock affords convenient space for a flight of steps descending gradually to the “dike”﻿—the local name for the embankment made at the foot of the cliffs to keep the Loire in its bed, and serve as a causeway for the high road from Paris to Nantes. At the top of the steps a gate opens upon a narrow stony footpath between two terraces, for here the soil is banked up, and walls are built to prevent landslips. These earthworks, as it were, are crowned with trellises and espaliers, so that the steep path that lies at the foot of the upper wall is almost hidden by the trees that grow on the top of the lower, upon which it lies. The view of the river widens out before you at every step as you climb to the house.
At the end you come to a second gateway, a Gothic archway covered with simple ornament, now crumbling into ruin and overgrown with wildflowers﻿—moss and ivy, wallflowers and pellitory. Every stone wall on the hillside is decked with this ineradicable plant-life, which springs up along the cracks afresh with new wreaths for every time of year.

===Chinese===

献给 D. W.
石榴居（La Grenadière）是卢瓦尔河右岸的一座小宅，顺流而下，在图尔（Tours）大桥下游约一英里处。这一带的河面宽得像湖，散布着绿色的洲渚，在两列崖岸之间流过；崖上，白石统一砌成的乡间宅邸立在各自的园子和葡萄园中间。世上最好的水果在那里向阳成熟。多少世代耐心的劳作在崖壁上开出一层层台地，使岩面映着阳光，热带的物产得以在户外、在人工的高温里生长。
---
一座教堂的尖顶从崖线一处较浅的洼处探出，标出圣西尔小村，那些散落的屋舍都隶属这个村子。再往前一点，舒瓦伊尔河穿过切进绵长低丘的一道肥沃山谷，注入卢瓦尔河。
石榴居在半山坡上，离教堂约百步，是那种有两三百年历史的老式房子，都兰每一处如画的地点都见得到。岩上一道裂缝恰好容得下一道石级，缓缓降到「堤」上——这是当地的叫法，指崖脚为约束卢瓦尔河床而筑的堤岸，兼作巴黎到南特的大路的路基。石级顶上一道门开向两片台地之间一条多石的窄径，因为这里的土壤壅成了埂，筑了墙防滑坡。这些土工，可以说，顶上攀着棚架和果树墙，所以贴着上墙脚的那条陡径，几乎叫长在下墙顶上的树木遮尽了。你一路登向宅子，河景在每一步上向你展开。
到头是第二道门，一座哥特式的拱门，带着朴素的装饰，如今已风蚀将圮，长满了野花——苔藓和常春藤，桂竹香和墙草。山坡上每一堵石墙都披着这铲除不尽的草木，它们顺着裂缝，一年一度抽出新编的花环。

===Original===

The worm-eaten gate gives into a little garden, a strip of turf, a few trees, and a wilderness of flowers and rose bushes﻿—a garden won from the rock on the highest terrace of all, with the dark, old balustrade along its edge. Opposite the gateway, a wooden summerhouse stands against the neighboring wall, the posts are covered with jessamine and honeysuckle, vines and clematis.
The house itself stands in the middle of this highest garden, above a vine-covered flight of steps, with an arched doorway beneath that leads to vast cellars hollowed out in the rock. All about the dwelling trellised vines and pomegranate-trees (the *grenadiers*, which give the name to the little close) are growing out in the open air. The front of the house consists of two large windows on either side of a very rustic-looking house door, and three dormer windows in the roof﻿—a slate roof with two gables, prodigiously high-pitched in proportion to the low ground-floor. The house walls are washed with yellow color; and door, and first-floor shutters, and the Venetian shutters of the attic windows, all are painted green.
Entering the house, you find yourself in a little lobby with a crooked staircase straight in front of you. It is a crazy wooden structure, the spiral balusters are brown with age, and the steps themselves take a new angle at every turn. The great old-fashioned paneled dining-room, floored with square white tiles from Château-Regnault, is on your right; to the left is the sitting-room, equally large, but here the walls are not paneled; they have been covered instead with a saffron-colored paper, bordered with green. The walnut-wood rafters are left visible, and the intervening spaces filled with a kind of white plaster.
The first story consists of two large whitewashed bedrooms with stone chimneypieces, less elaborately carved than those in the rooms beneath. Every door and window is on the south side of the house, save a single door to the north, contrived behind the staircase to give access to the vineyard. Against the western wall stands a supplementary timber-framed structure, all the woodwork exposed to the weather being fledged with slates, so that the walls are checkered with bluish lines. This shed (for it is little more) is the kitchen of the establishment.

===Chinese===

虫蛀的门里是一个小园子：一条草皮，几棵树，一片花木和蔷薇的荒莽——这是从岩石上夺来的园子，在最高一层台地上，沿边是一道暗色的老栏杆。门对面，一座木凉亭倚着邻墙，柱子上缠满茉莉和忍冬、葡萄和铁线莲。
宅子本身立在这最高的园子中央，在一道覆着葡萄的石级上方；级下有一个拱门，通向在岩石里掏出的深广的地窖。住宅四周，棚架上的葡萄和石榴树（grenadiers，这小园的名字便由此而来）长在露天下。宅子的正面是：当中一扇很乡土气的宅门，两边各两扇大窗，屋顶上开着三扇老虎窗——石板屋顶，两道山墙，同低矮的底层相比，坡度陡得出奇。宅墙刷成黄色；门、底楼的百叶窗和顶楼的威尼斯式百叶窗，一律漆成绿色。
走进宅子，是一小间门厅，迎面一道折角的楼梯。那是一座摇摇欲坠的木建筑，螺旋形的栏杆扶手因年月而发褐，踏步每转一折换一个角度。右边是那间老式的大镶板餐厅，铺着沙托-雷诺的白方砖；左边是同样大的起居室，只是这里墙不镶板，糊着一种藏红花色的纸，镶绿边。胡桃木的椽子露着，椽档里填一种白灰浆。
二层是两间粉刷过的大卧房，带石砌壁炉，雕饰不及楼下几间的讲究。宅子的门窗一律朝南，只有一扇北门，藏在楼梯背后，通葡萄园。西墙边搭着一座附加的木构架，凡露在风雨里的木料都挂了石板，墙面因此织着青灰的线条。这间披屋（它也不过是披屋）便是宅里的厨房。

===Original===

You can pass from it into the house without going outside; but, nevertheless, it boasts an entrance door of its own, and a short flight of steps that brings you to a deep well, and a very rustical-looking pump, half hidden by water-plants and savin bushes and tall grasses. The kitchen is a modern addition, proving beyond doubt that La Grenadière was originally nothing but a simple *vendangeoir*﻿—a vintage-house belonging to townsfolk in Tours, from which Saint-Cyr is separated by the vast riverbed of the Loire. The owners only came over for the day for a picnic, or at the vintage-time, sending provisions across in the morning, and scarcely ever spent the night there except during the grape harvest; but the English settled down on Touraine like a cloud of locusts, and La Grenadière must, of course, be completed if it was to find tenants. Luckily, however, this recent appendage is hidden from sight by the first two trees of a lime-tree avenue planted in a gully below the vineyards.
There are only two acres of vineyard at most, the ground rising at the back of the house so steeply that it is no very easy matter to scramble up among the vines. The slope, covered with green trailing shoots, ends within about five feet of the house wall in a ditch-like passage always damp and cold and full of strong growing green things, fed by the drainage of the highly cultivated ground above, for rainy weather washes down the manure into the garden on the terrace.
A vinedresser’s cottage also leans against the western gable, and is in some sort a continuation of the kitchen. Stone walls or espaliers surround the property, and all sorts of fruit-trees are planted among the vines; in short, not an inch of this precious soil is wasted. If by chance man overlooks some dry cranny in the rocks, Nature puts in a fig-tree, or sows wildflowers or strawberries in sheltered nooks among the stones.
Nowhere else in all the world will you find a human dwelling so humble and yet so imposing, so rich in fruit, and fragrant scents, and wide views of country. Here is a miniature Touraine in the heart of Touraine﻿—all its flowers and fruits and all the characteristic beauty of the land are fully represented.

===Chinese===

不出屋子就能从它进宅；可它偏还有自己一扇进门的门，和一小截台阶，引到一口深井和一个样子极土的水泵旁，半埋在水草、圆柏丛和高草里。厨房是后来添的，足证石榴居原先不过是一处简单的采葡萄屋（vendangeoir）——属于图尔城里市民的产业；图尔同圣西尔之间隔着卢瓦尔河宽阔的河床。主人只在白天过来野餐，或在采葡萄的时节过来，清早把吃食运过河，除葡萄收获期外几乎从不过夜；可是英国人像蝗群一样落满了都兰，石榴居要招得起租客，自然得配备齐全。所幸这新添的部分被葡萄园下一道冲沟里植的椴树的头两棵遮住了。
葡萄园至多不过两英亩，宅子背后的地面陡升，在葡萄棵子里攀爬不是容易的事。坡上覆满绿色的蔓条，离宅墙约五英尺处止于一条沟似的过道，常年阴冷潮湿，长满旺盛的绿色植物，靠上面精耕的地的排水滋养，因为雨天把肥料冲进下面台地的园子里。
一个葡萄园工人的小屋也倚着西山墙，多少算是厨房的延续。石墙和果树墙围着这份产业，葡萄行间种着各色果树；一言以蔽之，这宝贵的土壤一寸也不浪费。人若偶尔照看不到岩石的哪处干缝，自然便栽上一棵无花果，或在石间的荫角里播下野花和草莓。
普天之下，你再找不到一处人住的地方这样寒素、又这样气象堂堂，这样富于果实、芬芳和开阔的乡景。这里是都兰腹地的一座缩微都兰——它的花果，它的土地全部独特的美，样样齐备。

===Original===

Here are grapes of every district, figs and peaches and pears of every kind; melons are grown out of doors as easily as licorice plants, Spanish broom, Italian oleanders, and jessamines from the Azores. The Loire lies at your feet. You look down from the terrace upon the ever-changing river nearly two hundred feet below; and in the evening the breeze brings a fresh scent of the sea, with the fragrance of far-off flowers gathered upon its way. Some cloud wandering in space, changing its color and form at every moment as it crosses the pure blue of the sky, can alter every detail in the widespread wonderful landscape in a thousand ways, from every point of view. The eye embraces first of all the south bank of the Loire, stretching away as far as Amboise, then Tours with its suburbs and buildings, and the Plessis rising out of the fertile plain; further away, between Vouvray and Saint-Symphorien, you see a sort of crescent of gray cliff full of sunny vineyards; the only limits to your view are the low, rich hills along the Cher, a bluish line of horizon broken by many a château and the wooded masses of many a park. Out to the west you lose yourself in the immense river, where vessels come and go, spreading their white sails to the winds which seldom fail them in the wide Loire basin. A prince might build a summer palace at La Grenadière, but certainly it will always be the home of a poet’s desire, and the sweetest of retreats for two young lovers﻿—for this vintage house, which belongs to a substantial burgess of Tours, has charms for every imagination, for the humblest and dullest as well as for the most impassioned and lofty. No one can dwell there without feeling that happiness is in the air, without a glimpse of all that is meant by a peaceful life without care or ambition. There is that in the air and the sound of the river that sets you dreaming; the sands have a language, and are joyous or dreary, golden or wan; and the owner of the vineyard may sit motionless amid perennial flowers and tempting fruit, and feel all the stir of the world about him.
If an Englishman takes the house for the summer, he is asked a thousand francs for six months, the produce of the vineyard not included. If the tenant wishes for the orchard fruit, the rent is doubled; for the vintage, it is doubled again.

===Chinese===

这里有多地的葡萄，各样的无花果、桃子和梨；甜瓜在户外长得同甘草、西班牙金雀花、意大利夹竹桃和亚速尔茉莉一样容易。卢瓦尔河卧在你脚下。你从台地上俯瞰脚下近两百英尺处那条时时变幻的河；傍晚，微风带来海的新鲜气息，还带来一路收集的远方花朵的芬芳。一朵在空中游荡的云，每时每刻变换着颜色和形状，横过天空的纯蓝，能把这片广袤奇景的每个细节从每个观点千变万化地改写。眼睛先揽入卢瓦尔河南岸，一直伸到昂布瓦斯；再是图尔及其郊野屋宇，普莱西从肥沃的平原上升起；更远处，在武弗雷和圣桑福里安之间，你望见一带灰色崖壁的弧线，满是向阳的葡萄园；视野的尽头，只有谢尔河沿岸低而富的丘冈，一条青蓝的地平线，被多少座城堡和多少片园林的树丛断开。往西，你把自己迷失在大河里，船帆来往，向风张着白帆——在宽广的卢瓦尔河流域，风很少叫它们失望。一位亲王也尽可以在石榴居盖一座夏宫；可它必定永远是诗人意中的家，一对年轻情侣最甜的退隐地——因为这座属于图尔一位殷实市民的采葡萄屋，对每种想象都有魅力，对最早微迟钝的和对最热烈高尚的一样。谁住在那里，不能不感到幸福弥漫在空气里，不能不瞥见一种无忧无虑、无所企求的平静生活意味着的一切。空气和河声里有一样东西叫你入梦；沙滩有一种语言，时而欢畅时而凄凉，时而金黄时而苍白；葡萄园的主人尽可以坐在常开的花和诱人的果实中间一动不动，感到整个世界的骚动围绕着他。
倘若一个英国人租下这宅子避暑，六个月索价一千法郎，葡萄园的出产不计在内。租客若还要果园的水果，租金加倍；还要葡萄，再加一倍。

===Original===

What can La Grenadière be worth, you wonder; La Grenadière, with its stone staircase, its beaten path and triple terrace, its two acres of vineyard, its flowering roses about the balustrades, its worn steps, wellhead, rampant clematis, and cosmopolitan trees? It is idle to make a bid! La Grenadière will never be in the market; it was brought once and sold, but that was in 1690; and the owner parted with it for forty thousand francs, reluctant as any Arab of the desert to relinquish a favorite horse. Since then it has remained in the same family, its pride, its patrimonial jewel, its Regent diamond. “While you behold, you have and hold,” says the bard. And from La Grenadière you behold three valleys of Touraine and the cathedral towers aloft in air like a bit of filigree work. How can one pay for such treasures? Could one ever pay for the health recovered there under the linden-trees?
In the spring of one of the brightest years of the Restoration, a lady with her housekeeper and her two children (the oldest a boy thirteen years old, the youngest apparently about eight) came to Tours to look for a house. She saw La Grenadière and took it. Perhaps the distance from the town was an inducement to live there.
She made a bedroom of the drawing-room, gave the children the two rooms above, and the housekeeper slept in a closet behind the kitchen. The dining-room was sitting-room and drawing-room all in one for the little family. The house was furnished very simply but tastefully; there was nothing superfluous in it, and no trace of luxury. The walnut-wood furniture chosen by the stranger lady was perfectly plain, and the whole charm of the house consisted in its neatness and harmony with its surroundings.
It was rather difficult, therefore, to say whether the strange lady (Mme. Willemsens, as she styled herself) belonged to the upper middle or higher classes, or to an equivocal, unclassified feminine species. Her plain dress gave rise to the most contradictory suppositions, but her manners might be held to confirm those favorable to her. She had not lived at Saint-Cyr, moreover, for very long before her reserve excited the curiosity of idle people, who always, and especially in the country, watch anybody or anything that promises to bring some interest into their narrow lives.
Mme. Willemsens was rather tall; she was thin and slender, but delicately shaped.

===Chinese===

石榴居值多少钱，你要问；它有石级，有踏出的小径和三层台地，有两英亩葡萄园，栏杆边开着蔷薇，有磨旧的台阶、井台、蔓生的铁线莲和世界各处的树？出价是多余的！石榴居永远不会上市；它被买卖过一次，但那是一六九〇年的事；主人四万法郎出手，恋恋不舍，像沙漠里的阿拉伯人让出心爱的马。从此它留在同一家族手里，是家族的骄傲，是祖传的珠宝，是他们的「摄政王」钻石。「你看见了，便是你的」，诗人这样说。而从石榴居上，你看见都兰的三条河谷，看见高擎在空中的大教堂塔尖，像一件金银丝的细工。这样的珍宝怎样付得起钱？在那些椴树底下寻回的健康，又怎样付得起？
王政复辟（the Restoration）年间最明媚的年份之一的一个春天，一位夫人带着她的女管家和两个孩子（大的男孩十三岁，小的看样子八岁上下）来到图尔找房子。她看中了石榴居，租下了。也许离城有一段路，正是住下去的一个诱因。
她把起居室改作卧房，把楼上的两间给孩子，女管家睡厨房后头一间小间。餐厅便一身兼任这一小家的起居室和客厅。宅子布置得很简单但有品味；没有一件多余的东西，不见一点奢侈的痕迹。这位陌生夫人选的胡桃木家具十分朴素，宅子全部的魅力在于它的整洁和同四周的和谐。
因此，很难说这位陌生的夫人（她自称维莱姆桑夫人）属于上层市民或更高的阶级，还是属于一种暧昧的、无以归类的女性。她素净的衣裳引出最矛盾的猜测，可她的仪态却可以认作支持那些有利于她的猜测。况且她在圣西尔住得不久，她的深藏便激起了闲人们的好奇——闲人们永远、尤其是在乡下，盯着任何一个许诺给他们的窄生活带来一点兴味的人或事。
维莱姆桑夫人相当高；她瘦而纤细，但形体纤秀。

===Original===

She had pretty feet, more remarkable for the grace of her instep and ankle than for the more ordinary merit of slenderness; her gloved hands, too, were shapely. There were flitting patches of deep red in a pale face, which must have been fresh and softly colored once. Premature wrinkles had withered the delicately modeled forehead beneath the coronet of soft, well-set chestnut hair, invariably wound about her head in two plaits, a girlish coiffure which suited the melancholy face. There was a deceptive look of calm in the dark eyes, with the hollow, shadowy circles about them; sometimes, when she was off her guard, their expression told of secret anguish. The oval of her face was somewhat long; but happiness and health had perhaps filled and perfected the outlines. A forced smile, full of quiet sadness, hovered continually on her pale lips; but when the children, who were always with her, looked up at their mother, or asked one of the incessant idle questions which convey so much to a mother’s ears, then the smile brightened, and expressed the joys of a mother’s love. Her gait was slow and dignified. Her dress never varied; evidently she had made up her mind to think no more of her toilette, and to forget a world by which she meant no doubt to be forgotten. She wore a long, black gown, confined at the waist by a watered-silk ribbon, and by way of scarf a lawn handkerchief with a broad hem, the two ends passed carelessly through her waistband. The instinct of dress showed itself in that she was daintily shod, and gray silk stockings carried out the suggestion of mourning in this unvarying costume. Lastly, she always wore a bonnet after the English fashion, always of the same shape and the same gray material, and a black veil. Her health apparently was extremely weak; she looked very ill. On fine evenings she would take her only walk, down to the bridge of Tours, bringing the two children with her to breathe the fresh, cool air along the Loire, and to watch the sunset effects on a landscape as wide as the Bay of Naples or the Lake of Geneva.
During the whole time of her stay at La Grenadière she went but twice into Tours; once to call on the headmaster of the school, to ask him to give her the names of the best masters of Latin, drawing, and mathematics; and a second time to make arrangements for the children’s lessons.

===Chinese===

她有一双好看的脚，足弓和脚踝的秀美比寻常的纤瘦更惹眼；戴手套的手也秀气。苍白的脸上飞着几片深红，那张脸当年想必新鲜柔艳。早生的皱纹萎谢了那用心雕琢的额头，额上一顶栗色软发的冠，那头发永远在头上盘成两条辫子，一种少女的发式，正配这张忧郁的脸。深色的眼睛里有一种貌似平静的神色，眼周是凹陷的阴影圈；有时她一不留神，眼里的表情便泄露了暗藏的苦楚。她的脸型椭圆略长；可是幸福和健康也许曾经把轮廓填满、补足。一个强作的微笑，盛满安静的哀愁，时时浮在她苍白的唇上；可当那总在她身边的孩子们仰脸望母亲，或问出那些没完没了的闲问题——在母亲耳朵里却有那么多的意思——微笑便亮起来，表达出母爱的欢喜。她步态缓慢而端庄。她的装束从不变化；显然她已拿定主意不再想梳妆，要忘掉一个她无疑也想被它忘掉的世界。她穿一件黑色长裙，腰间束一条波纹缎带，充作披肩的是一方阔边的细麻手帕，两角随意掖在腰带里。装扮的本能表现在：她的鞋讲究，灰丝袜把这身不变的丧服的点题又续了一层。末了，她永远戴一顶英国式软帽，永远同一个样式、同一种灰料子，加一幅黑纱。她的健康显然极弱；她看上去病得很重。晴朗的傍晚，她做她唯一的散步，走到图尔大桥，带着两个孩子，沿卢瓦尔河呼吸清凉的空气，看日落在一片同那不勒斯湾或日内瓦湖一样宽的风景上的效果。
她住在石榴居的全部时间里，只进过两次图尔城：一次去拜访中学校长，请他告诉她最好的拉丁文、图画和数学教师的名字；再一次是安排孩子们的功课。

===Original===

But her appearance on the bridge of an evening, once or twice a week, was quite enough to excite the interest of almost all the inhabitants of Tours, who make a regular promenade of the bridge. Still, in spite of a kind of spy system, by which no harm is meant, a provincial habit bred of want of occupation and the restless inquisitiveness of the principal society, nothing was known for certain of the newcomer’s rank, fortune, or real condition. Only, the owner of La Grenadière told one or two of his friends that the name under which the stranger had signed the lease (her real name, therefore, in all probability) was Augusta Willemsens, Countess of Brandon. This, of course, must be her husband’s name. Events, which will be narrated in their place, confirmed this revelation; but it went no further than the little world of men of business known to the landlord.
So Madame Willemsens was a continual mystery to people of condition. Hers was no ordinary nature; her manners were simple and delightfully natural, the tones of her voice were divinely sweet﻿—this was all that she suffered others to discover. In her complete seclusion, her sadness, her beauty so passionately obscured, nay, almost blighted, there was so much to charm, that several young gentlemen fell in love; but the more sincere the lover, the more timid he became; and besides, the lady inspired awe, and it was a difficult matter to find enough courage to speak to her. Finally, if a few of the bolder sort wrote to her, their letters must have been burned unread. It was Mme. Willemsens’ practice to throw all the letters which she received into the fire, as if she meant that the time spent in Touraine should be untroubled by any outside cares even of the slightest. She might have come to the enchanting retreat to give herself up wholly to the joy of living.
The three masters whose presence was allowed at La Grenadière spoke with something like admiring reverence of the touching picture that they saw there of the close, unclouded intimacy of the life led by this woman and the children.
The two little boys also aroused no small interest. Mothers could not see them without a feeling of envy. Both children were like Mme. Willemsens, who was, in fact, their mother.

===Chinese===

可是她一星期一两次在傍晚出现在桥上，已足够引起几乎全图尔居民的关切——他们把大桥当作固定的散步场。尽管有一种不算恶意的探察——外省的习惯，闲得无聊加上上流社会的刨根问底——人们对这位新来者的门第、财产和真实境况始终没有确凿的了解。只有石榴居的主人对他的一两个朋友说过，陌生人签租约用的名字（因此多半是她的真名）是奥古斯塔·维莱姆桑，布兰登伯爵夫人。这当然该是她丈夫的姓氏。后文将要叙到的事证实了这一透露；可它没有越出房东认识的那个小小的生意人的圈子。
于是维莱姆桑夫人对有身份的人们始终是个谜。她不是个寻常的天性；她的仪态简单而可爱地自然，她声音的音色甜得近乎神圣——这便是她容许旁人发现的全部。在她全然的幽居里，在她的哀愁里，在她那样炽烈地遮掩、几乎摧折的美貌里，有那样多的动人处，以致好几位年轻绅士堕入了情网；可是情人愈真挚，愈胆怯；况且这位夫人令人敬畏，要鼓起足够的勇气同她说话是件难事。末了，倘若几个胆大的写了信，那些信想必没有拆便烧掉了。维莱姆桑夫人的习惯是把收到的一切信件扔进火里，仿佛她要让住在都兰的这一段时光，不受外界哪怕最轻微的烦扰。她来这迷人的隐居地，或许是把自己完全交给活着的欢乐。
获准进石榴居的三位教师，怀着近乎敬畏的赞叹，谈起他们在这位妇人和孩子们身上看到的那幅动人的图景——那种亲密无间、毫无阴翳的共同生活。
两个小男孩也引起不小的兴趣。母亲们见了他们不能不眼热。两个孩子都像维莱姆桑夫人——事实上，她正是他们的母亲。

===Original===

They had the transparent complexion and bright color, the clear, liquid eyes, the long lashes, the fresh outlines, the dazzling characteristics of childish beauty.
The elder, Louis-Gaston, had dark hair and fearless eyes. Everything about him spoke as plainly of robust, physical health as his broad, high brow, with its gracious curves, spoke of energy of character. He was quick and alert in his movements, and strong of limb, without a trace of awkwardness. Nothing took him unawares, and he seemed to think about everything that he saw.
Marie-Gaston, the other child, had hair that was almost golden, though a lock here and there had deepened to the mother’s chestnut tint. Marie-Gaston was slender; he had the delicate features and the subtle grace so charming in Mme. Willemsens. He did not look strong. There was a gentle look in his gray eyes; his face was pale, there was something feminine about the child. He still wore his hair in long, wavy curls, and his mother would not have him give up embroidered collars, and little jackets fastened with frogs and spindle-shaped buttons; evidently she took a thoroughly feminine pleasure in the costume, a source of as much interest to the mother as to the child. The elder boy’s plain white collar, turned down over a closely fitting jacket, made a contrast with his brother’s clothing, but the color and material were the same; the two brothers were otherwise dressed alike, and looked alike.
No one could see them without feeling touched by the way in which Louis took care of Marie. There was an almost fatherly look in the older boy’s eyes; and Marie, child though he was, seemed to be full of gratitude to Louis. They were like two buds, scarcely separated from the stem that bore them, swayed by the same breeze, lying in the same ray of sunlight; but the one was a brightly colored flower, the other somewhat bleached and pale. At a glance, a word, an inflection in their mother’s voice, they grew heedful, turned to look at her and listened, and did at once what they were bidden, or asked, or recommended to do. Mme. Willemsens had so accustomed them to understand her wishes and desires, that the three seemed to have their thoughts in common.

===Chinese===

他们有透明的肤色和鲜亮的血色，清澈水灵的眼睛，长长的睫毛，新鲜的轮廓，童年的美那些炫目的特质。
大的路易-加斯东，深色头发，无所畏惧的眼睛。他身上的一切同他宽高的额头一样明白地诉说着体魄的强健——那额头带着雍容的曲线，诉说着性格的刚毅。他动作敏捷机警，四肢有力，没有一点笨拙。什么都瞒不过他，他似乎对他看见的每样东西都要想一想。
另一个孩子玛丽-加斯东，头发近乎金黄，不过一绺一绺间杂着母亲的栗色。玛丽-加斯东纤细；他有维莱姆桑夫人那样清秀的五官和精微的风韵。他看上去不壮。灰眼睛里有一种温柔的神色；他脸色苍白，这孩子身上有一点女性的东西。他还留着长长的鬈发，母亲不肯他放弃绣花领子，和用盘花扣和纺锤形纽子扣住的小外衣；显然她从这身装束里得到一种十足女性的乐趣，这乐趣于母亲于孩子是同等的兴味。大孩子翻在紧身上衣外的素白领子，同弟弟的衣裳形成对照，可颜色料子是一样的；兄弟俩此外穿戴相同，相貌相像。
谁见了他们，不能不为路易照料玛丽的样子所感动。大孩子的眼睛里有一种近乎父辈的神色；而玛丽，虽还是孩子，似乎对路易满怀感激。他们像两朵蓓蕾，还没有同承载他们的枝干分开，同一阵风里摇曳，同一线阳光里躺着；只是一朵是鲜色的花，一朵略显得白淡。母亲的一个眼色、一句话、一个转调，他们便凝神起来，转头望她，听着，立刻去照吩咐、请求或劝告的做。维莱姆桑夫人那样叫他们惯于领会她的意愿和心愿，以致三个人的心思似乎浑然一体。

===Original===

When they went for a walk, and the children, absorbed in their play, ran away to gather a flower or to look at some insect, she watched them with such deep tenderness in her eyes, that the most indifferent passerby would feel moved, and stop and smile at the children, and give the mother a glance of friendly greeting. Who would not have admired the dainty neatness of their dress, their sweet, childish voices, the grace of their movements, the promise in their faces, the innate something that told of careful training from the cradle? They seemed as if they had never shed tears nor wailed like other children. Their mother knew, as it were, by electrically swift intuition, the desires and the pains which she anticipated and relieved. She seemed to dread a complaint from one of them more than the loss of her soul. Everything in her children did honor to their mother’s training. Their threefold life, seemingly one life, called up vague, fond thoughts; it was like a vision of the dreamed-of bliss of a better world. And the three, so attuned to each other, lived in truth such a life as one might picture for them at first sight﻿—the ordered, simple, and regular life best suited for a child’s education.
Both children rose an hour after daybreak and repeated a short prayer, a habit learned in their babyhood. For seven years the sincere petition had been put up every morning on their mother’s bed, and begun and ended by a kiss. Then the two brothers went through their morning toilet as scrupulously as any pretty woman; doubtless they had been trained in habits of minute attention to the person, so necessary to health of body and mind, habits in some sort conducive to a sense of wellbeing. Conscientiously they went through their duties, so afraid were they lest their mother should say when she kissed them at breakfast-time, “My darling children, where can you have been to have such black fingernails already?” Then the two went out into the garden and shook off the dreams of the night in the morning air and dew, until sweeping and dusting operations were completed, and they could learn their lessons in the sitting-room until their mother joined them.

===Chinese===

他们出去散步，孩子们玩得入神，跑开去采一朵花或看一只虫，她望着他们的眼睛里盛着那样深的温柔，连最漠然的过路人也要动情，停下来朝孩子们微笑，给母亲一个友善致意的眼色。谁不欣赏他们衣装的雅洁，他们甜甜的童音，他们动作的风韵，他们脸上的前程，那种从摇篮里就受着细心调教的先天标记？他们仿佛从来不曾像别的孩子那样哭过闹过。他们的母亲仿佛凭着电光一样快的直觉，就知道他们的愿望和痛楚，预先替他们排解。她似乎怕他们的一声抱怨甚于怕失去自己的灵魂。她孩子们身上的一切都为母亲的教养增光。三个人的三重生活俨然一个生命，唤起朦胧的怜爱之思；像一幅更好世界里梦寐以求的至福的幻象。而这三个这样互相调谐的人，过的也确实是一见之下就能为他们设想的那种生活——最有益于孩子教育的、有秩序、简单而规律的生活。
两个孩子天亮后一个钟头起身，背一段短祷文——襁褓里学会的习惯。七年来，这个诚挚的祈祷每天早晨在母亲的床前献上，以一个吻开始，以一个吻结束。随后兄弟俩像任何一个俏丽的女人一样一丝不苟地做晨间的梳洗；无疑他们被训练出了对个人仪容 minutely 照料的习惯——于身心之健康如此必要、又在某种意义上滋养着舒适感的习惯。他们认真地履行这些职责，生怕母亲在早餐时吻他们说：「我的宝贝们，你们到底去了哪儿，指甲已经这么黑了？」随后两人到园子里去，在清晨的空气和露水里抖落夜里的梦，直到打扫抹拭完毕，能在起居室里学习功课，等母亲来同他们会合。

===Original===

But although it was understood that they must not go to their mother’s room before a certain hour, they peeped in at the door continually; and these morning inroads, made in defiance of the original compact, were delicious moments for all three. Marie sprang upon the bed to put his arms around his idolized mother, and Louis, kneeling by the pillow, took her hand in his. Then came inquiries, anxious as a lover’s, followed by angelic laughter, passionate childish kisses, eloquent silences, lisping words, and the little ones’ stories interrupted and resumed by a kiss, stories seldom finished, though the listener’s interest never failed.
“Have you been industrious?” their mother would ask, but in tones so sweet and so kindly that she seemed ready to pity laziness as a misfortune, and to glance through tears at the child who was satisfied with himself.
She knew that the thought of pleasing her put energy into the children’s work; and they knew that their mother lived for them, and that all her thoughts and her time were given to them. A wonderful instinct, neither selfishness nor reason, perhaps the first innocent beginnings of sentiment teaches children to know whether or not they are the first and sole thought, to find out those who love to think of them and for them. If you really love children, the dear little ones, with open hearts and unerring sense of justice, are marvelously ready to respond to love. Their love knows passion and jealousy and the most gracious delicacy of feeling; they find the tenderest words of expression; they trust you﻿—put an entire belief in you. Perhaps there are no undutiful children without undutiful mothers, for a child’s affection is always in proportion to the affection that it receives﻿—in early care, in the first words that it hears, in the response of the eyes to which a child first looks for love and life. All these things draw them closer to the mother or drive them apart. God lays the child under the mother’s heart, that she may learn that for a long time to come her heart must be its home. And yet﻿—there are mothers cruelly slighted, mothers whose sublime, pathetic tenderness meets only a harsh return, a hideous ingratitude which shows how difficult it is to lay down hard-and-fast rules in matters of feeling.
Here, not one of all the thousand heart ties that bind child and mother had been broken.

===Chinese===

可是虽说讲定了某一个钟点之前不许去母亲房里，他们还是不住地在门口张望；这些违背原约的清晨突袭，于三个人都是甜美的时刻。玛丽扑上床去搂住他崇拜的母亲，路易跪在枕边，把她的手握在自己手里。随后是情人一般焦切的问询，接着是天使般的笑声，热烈的孩子的亲吻，意味深长的静默，咿呀的语声，小家伙们讲的故事被一个吻打断又接上——故事很少有讲完的时候，听的人的兴趣却从不衰减。
「你们用功了么？」母亲会问，可声调那样甜、那样和善，仿佛她打算把懒惰当作一件不幸来怜悯，含着泪看重那个心满意足的孩子。
她知道讨她欢喜的心思给孩子们的功课添了劲；他们也知道母亲为他们活着，她全部的心思和时间都给了他们。一种奇妙的本能——既非自私也非理智，也许是感情的最初的无辜的开端——教孩子们知道他们是不是一个人第一且唯一的牵挂，教他们认出那些乐于想着他们、替他们着想的人。倘若你真爱孩子，这些亲爱的小人儿，怀着敞开的心和不出错的正义感，会以奇妙的速度回应爱。他们的爱里有激情，有嫉妒，有最温雅的细腻；他们找得到最温柔的言辞；他们信任你——对你怀着一整个的信念。世上或许没有不孝的孩子而没有不孝的母亲，因为孩子的爱永远同它领受的爱成比例——在早期的照料里，在他听见的最初的话语里，在他首先寻觅爱与生命的眼睛的回应里。这一切把他们拉近母亲，或推远。上帝把孩子放在母亲的心下，好教她知道：往后很长的岁月里，她的心必须是孩子的家。然而——也有惨遭轻慢的母亲，有母亲的崇高悲怆的温柔只换来苛酷的回报、可憎的忘恩的——这忘恩说明，要在感情的事上立下刻板的规则多么难。
在这里，维系孩子与母亲的千百条心的纽带，没有一条断过。

===Original===

The three were alone in the world; they lived one life, a life of close sympathy. If Mme. Willemsens was silent in the morning, Louis and Marie would not speak, respecting everything in her, even those thoughts which they did not share. But the older boy, with a precocious power of thought, would not rest satisfied with his mother’s assertion that she was perfectly well. He scanned her face with uneasy forebodings; the exact danger he did not know, but dimly he felt it threatening in those purple rings about her eyes, in the deepening hollows under them, and the feverish red that deepened in her face. If Marie’s play began to tire her, his sensitive tact was quick to discover this, and he would call to his brother:
“Come, Marie! let us run in to breakfast, I am hungry!”
But when they reached the door, he would look back to catch the expression on his mother’s face. She still could find a smile for him, nay, often there were tears in her eyes when some little thing revealed her child’s exquisite feeling, a too early comprehension of sorrow.
Mme. Willemsens dressed during the children’s early breakfast and game of play; she was coquettish for her darlings; she wished to be pleasing in their eyes; for them she would fain be in all things lovely, a gracious vision, with the charm of some sweet perfume of which one can never have enough.
She was always dressed in time to hear their lessons, which lasted from ten till three, with an interval at noon for lunch, the three taking the meal together in the summerhouse. After lunch the children played for an hour, while she﻿—poor woman and happy mother﻿—lay on a long sofa in the summerhouse, so placed that she could look out over the soft, ever-changing country of Touraine, a land that you learn to see afresh in all the thousand chance effects produced by daylight and sky and the time of year.
The children scampered through the orchard, scrambled about the terraces, chased the lizards, scarcely less nimble than they; investigating flowers and seeds and insects, continually referring all questions to their mother, running to and fro between the garden and the summerhouse. Children have no need of toys in the country, everything amuses them.
Mme. Willemsens sat at her embroidery during their lessons.

===Chinese===

这三个人在世上相依为命；他们过着一个生活，一个深相感应的生活。倘若维莱姆桑夫人早晨沉默，路易和玛丽便不说话，敬重她身上的一切，连他们不分享的那些心思也敬重。可那个大孩子，带着早熟的思想力，不满足于母亲自称安好的话。他怀着不安的预感细察她的脸；确切的危险他不知道，可他朦胧地感到它威胁着——在眼下那些青紫的圈里，在眼下愈陷愈深的凹窝里，在她脸上愈来愈深的烧热的红晕里。倘若玛丽的玩耍开始使她疲倦，他敏感的机智立刻察觉，便喊他的弟弟：
「来，玛丽！我们跑进去吃早饭吧，我饿了！」
可到了门口，他还要回头去捉母亲脸上的表情。她还找得出一个微笑给他；不，往往她眼里含着泪，当某件小事显出她孩子那分精致的感情、那分对忧伤的太早的了悟。
维莱姆桑夫人趁孩子们清晨用早餐、玩耍时梳妆；她为她的宝贝们卖俏；她愿在他们眼睛里是好看的；为了他们，她甘愿事事可爱，做一个温婉的幻象，带着一种闻不厌的甜香。
她永远及时穿好，好听孩子们的功课；功课从十点到三点，正午歇一歇用午餐，三个人一同在凉亭里吃。午饭后孩子们玩一个钟头，她——可怜的女人，幸福的母亲——躺在凉亭里一张长榻上，榻放的位置正好望得见都兰柔和的、时时变幻的原野——那片土地，你学会在日光、天空和季节的一千种偶然效果里重新看见它。
孩子们在果园里奔跑，在台地上爬上爬下，追壁虎——它们比孩子们的灵巧差不了多少；考察花、种子和虫子，把一切问题不断提给母亲，在园子和凉亭之间跑来跑去。乡下的孩子不需要玩具，样样都逗他们喜欢。
孩子们上课时，维莱姆桑夫人坐在一旁做刺绣。

===Original===

She never spoke, nor did she look at masters or pupils; but she followed attentively all that was said, striving to gather the sense of the words to gain a general idea of Louis’ progress. If Louis asked a question that puzzled his master, his mother’s eyes suddenly lighted up, and she would smile and glance at him with hope in her eyes. Of Marie she asked little. Her desire was with her eldest son. Already she treated him, as it were, respectfully, using all a woman’s, all a mother’s tact to arouse the spirit of high endeavor in the boy, to teach him to think of himself as capable of great things. She did this with a secret purpose, which Louis was to understand in the future; nay, he understood it already.
Always, the lesson over, she went as far as the gate with the master, and asked strict account of Louis’ progress. So kindly and so winning was her manner, that his tutors told her the truth, pointing out where Louis was weak, so that she might help him in his lessons. Then came dinner, and play after dinner, then a walk, and lessons were learned till bedtime.
So their days went. It was a uniform but full life; work and amusements left them not a dull hour in the day. Discouragement and quarreling were impossible. The mother’s boundless love made everything smooth. She taught her little sons moderation by refusing them nothing, and submission by making them see underlying Necessity in its many forms; she put heart into them with timely praise; developing and strengthening all that was best in their natures with the care of a good fairy. Tears sometimes rose to her burning eyes as she watched them play, and thought how they had never caused her the slightest vexation. Happiness so far-reaching and complete brings such tears, because for us it represents the dim imaginings of Heaven which we all of us form in our minds.
Those were delicious hours spent on that sofa in the garden-house, in looking out on sunny days over the wide stretches of river and the picturesque landscape, listening to the sound of her children’s voices as they laughed at their own laughter, to the little quarrels that told most plainly of their union of heart, of Louis’ paternal care of Marie, of the love that both of them felt for her.

===Chinese===

她从不说话，也不看教师和学生；可她专注地跟着一切所说的话，努力抓住字句的意思，好对路易的进境得到一个总的概念。倘若路易问出一个难住教师的问题，母亲的眼睛忽然亮起来，她便微笑着，带着希望的神色望他一眼。对玛丽她问得少。她的心愿系在长子身上。她已经在某种程度上恭敬地待他，用一个女人全部的、一个母亲全部的机敏，唤起这男孩奋发的志气，教他把自己看作能成大事的人。她这样做怀着一种隐秘的用意，路易日后自会懂得；不，他已经懂得了。
功课一完，她永远送教师到门口，对路易的进步严格地问个明白。她的态度那样和善、那样动人，以至导师们对她说实话，指出路易哪里薄弱，好让她在功课上帮他。随后是正餐，餐后的玩耍，再是散步，然后背功课直到就寝。
他们的日子就这样过。那是一种划一却充实的生活；功课和消遣使他们一天里没有一个沉闷的钟点。沮丧与争吵在这里不可能。母亲无边的大爱把一切都熨平了。她什么都不拒绝，以此教两个小儿子节制；她让他们看见多面的必然，以此教他们顺从；她用应时的夸奖给他们添勇气；像一个善良的仙女，悉心培育和加强他们天性里最好的一切。她看着他们玩耍，想到他们从不曾给她一点烦恼，热灼的眼睛里有时涌上泪来。这样深广完全的幸福带来这样的泪，因为在我们，它代表着我们人人心里对天堂的朦胧想象。
那些在园亭那张长榻上度过的钟点是甜美的：晴日里望着宽阔的河面和如画的风景，听孩子们的语声——他们对自己的笑声发笑，听那些小小的拌嘴——最明白地说出他们心灵的契合，路易对玛丽父辈般的照料，和两个孩子对她共同的爱。

===Original===

They spoke English and French equally well (they had had an English nurse since their babyhood), so their mother talked to them in both languages; directing the bent of their childish minds with admirable skill, admitting no fallacious reasoning, no bad principle. She ruled by kindness, concealing nothing, explaining everything. If Louis wished for books, she was careful to give him interesting yet accurate books﻿—books of biography, the lives of great seamen, great captains, and famous men, for little incidents in their history gave her numberless opportunities of explaining the world and life to her children. She would point out the ways in which men, really great in themselves, had risen from obscurity; how they had started from the lowest ranks of society, with no one to look to but themselves, and achieved noble destinies.
These readings, and they were not the least useful of Louis’ lessons, took place while little Marie slept on his mother’s knee in the quiet of the summer night, and the Loire reflected the sky; but when they ended, this adorable woman’s sadness always seemed to be doubled; she would cease to speak, and sit motionless and pensive, and her eyes would fill with tears.
“Mother, why are you crying?” Louis asked one balmy June evening, just as the twilight of a soft-lit night succeeded to a hot day.
Deeply moved by his trouble, she put her arm about the child’s neck and drew him to her.
“Because, my boy, the lot of Jameray Duval, the poor and friendless lad who succeeded at last, will be your lot, yours and your brother’s, and I have brought it upon you. Before very long, dear child, you will be alone in the world, with no one to help or befriend you. While you are still children, I shall leave you, and yet, if only I could wait till you are big enough and know enough to be Marie’s guardian! But I shall not live so long. I love you so much that it makes me very unhappy to think of it. Dear children, if only you do not curse me some day!﻿—”
“But why should I curse you some day, mother?”
“Some day,” she said, kissing him on the forehead, “you will find out that I have wronged you. I am going to leave you, here, without money, without”﻿—and she hesitated﻿—“without a father,” she added, and at the word she burst into tears and put the boy from her gently.

===Chinese===

他们英语法语说得一样好（他们从小有一个英国奶妈），母亲便用两种语言同他们交谈；以可钦的技巧引导他们童心的趋向，不容一点谬误的推理、一条坏的原则进来。她以仁慈施行统治，什么都不瞒，样样都解释。路易若要书，她小心给他有趣而可靠的书——传记类的书，大航海家、大将帅和名人的传，因为它们历史里的小事件，给她无数的机会向孩子们解释世界和人生。她会指出那些自身真正伟大的人怎样从微贱中升起；怎样从社会的最底层起步，除了自己没有人可以仰仗，而成就了高贵的命运。
这样的阅读——它们并非路易功课里最无用的部分——进行的时候，小玛丽常在静谧的夏夜睡在母亲膝上，卢瓦尔河映着天空；可是一到读完，这位可爱的人的哀愁仿佛总是加倍了；她便不再言语，一动不动地坐着出神，眼睛里充满泪水。
「妈妈，你为什么哭？」一个温和的六月傍晚，路易问——那时，一个光线柔和的夜的薄暮刚接上一个炎热的日子。
她被他的烦恼深深打动，伸出臂膀搂住孩子的脖子，把他拉到身边。
「因为，我的孩子，雅姆雷·杜瓦尔——那个贫苦无依、末了成功了的少年——的命运，将是你的命运，你和你弟弟的命运，而这是我带给你们的。不久以后，亲爱的孩子，你就要独自在世上，没有人帮助，没有人亲近。你们还是孩子的时候，我就要丢下你们了；可我若能等到你长得够大、懂得够多、能做玛丽的保护人，该多好！可我活不了那么久。我爱你们爱得这样厉害，一想起来就非常难过。亲爱的孩子们，只要你们将来有一天不要咒我！——」
「可我为什么有一天要咒你呢，妈妈？」
「有一天，」她说着，吻他的额头，「你会发现我害了你们。我要把你们丢在这里，没有钱，没有——」她迟疑了一下——「没有父亲，」她添了一句；说到这个词，她的眼泪迸出来，轻轻把孩子从身边推开。

===Original===

A sort of intuition told Louis that his mother wished to be alone, and he carried off Marie, now half awake. An hour later, when his brother was in bed, he stole down and out to the summerhouse where his mother was sitting.
“Louis! come here.”
The words were spoken in tones delicious to his heart. The boy sprang to his mother’s arms, and the two held each other in an almost convulsive embrace.
“*Chérie*,” he said at last, the name by which he often called her, finding that even loving words were too weak to express his feeling, “*chérie*, why are you afraid that you are going to die?”
“I am ill, my poor darling; every day I am losing strength, and there is no cure for my illness; I know that.”
“What is the matter with you?”
“Something that I ought to forget; something that you must never know.﻿—You must not know what caused my death.”
The boy was silent for a while. He stole a glance now and again at his mother; and she, with her eyes raised to the sky, was watching the clouds. It was a sad, sweet moment. Louis could not believe that his mother would die soon, but instinctively he felt trouble which he could not guess. He respected her long musings. If he had been rather older, he would have read happy memories blended with thoughts of repentance, the whole story of a woman’s life in that sublime face﻿—the careless childhood, the loveless marriage, a terrible passion, flowers springing up in storm and struck down by the thunderbolt into an abyss from which there is no return.
“Darling mother,” Louis said at last, “why do you hide your pain from me?”
“My boy, we ought to hide our troubles from strangers,” she said; “we should show them a smiling face, never speak of ourselves to them, nor think about ourselves; and these rules, put in practice in family life, conduce to its happiness. You will have much to bear one day! Ah me! then think of your poor mother who died smiling before your eyes, hiding her sufferings from you, and you will take courage to endure the ills of life.”
She choked back her tears, and tried to make the boy understand the mechanism of existence, the value of money, the standing and consideration that it gives, and its bearing on social position; the honorable means of gaining a livelihood, and the necessity of a training.

===Chinese===

一种直觉告诉路易，母亲想独自待着，他便把半醒的玛丽抱走了。一个钟头后，弟弟上了床，他溜下楼，出到园亭，母亲正坐在那里。
「路易！过来。」
这几个字的声调甜蜜透心。孩子扑进母亲的怀抱，两个几乎是痉挛地拥在一处。
「亲爱的，」他终于开口——他常这样叫她，觉得连爱这样的字眼都太轻，盛不下他的感情——「亲爱的，你为什么怕自己要死？」
「我病着，我可怜的宝贝；我的气力一天天失去，我的病没有治法；这我知道。」
「你得了什么病？」
「一件我应当忘掉的事；一件你永远不能知道的事。——你不能知道我的死因。」
孩子沉默了一会儿。他不时偷看母亲一眼；她呢，眼睛望着天，正看云。那是一个悲哀而甜美的时刻。路易不能相信母亲快死了，可他本能地感到一种他猜不出的烦乱。他敬重她的悠长的沉思。他若再大几岁，就会在那张崇高的脸上读出同悔恨交织的幸福回忆，读出一个女人一生的全部故事——无忧的童年，无爱的婚姻，一场可怕的激情，风暴里开出的花，被雷殛落，坠入一个无法回头的深渊。
「亲爱的妈妈，」路易终于说，「你为什么把你的痛苦瞒着我？」
「我的孩子，我们应当把烦恼瞒着外人，」她说；「我们该给他们看一张笑脸，不同他们谈自己，也不去想自己；这些规矩，拿到家庭生活里实行，有助于家庭的幸福。有一天你有许多要忍受的！唉！那时想想你可怜的母亲，她在你眼前含笑死去，把她的苦痛瞒着你，你就有勇气承受人生的祸患了。」
她咽住泪，试着让孩子懂得生存的机制，金钱的价值，它给予的地位和体面，它同社会身份的关系；谋生的体面的手段，和受一种训练的必要。

===Original===

Then she told him that one of the chief causes of her sadness and her tears was the thought that, on the morrow of her death, he and Marie would be left almost resourceless, with but a slender stock of money, and no friend but God.
“How quick I must be about learning!” cried Louis, giving her a piteous, searching look.
“Oh! how happy I am!” she said, showering kisses and tears on her son. “He understands me!﻿—Louis,” she went on, “you will be your brother’s guardian, will you not? You promise me that? You are no longer a child!”
“Yes, I promise,” he said; “but you are not going to die yet﻿—say that you are not going to die!”
“Poor little ones!” she replied, “love for you keeps the life in me. And this country is so sunny, the air is so bracing, perhaps﻿—”
“You make me love Touraine more than ever,” said the child.
From that day, when Mme. Willemsens, foreseeing the approach of death, spoke to Louis of his future, he concentrated his attention on his work, grew more industrious, and less inclined to play than heretofore. When he had coaxed Marie to read a book and to give up boisterous games, there was less noise in the hollow pathways and gardens and terraced walks of La Grenadière. They adapted their lives to their mother’s melancholy. Day by day her face was growing pale and wan, there were hollows now in her temples, the lines in her forehead grew deeper night after night.
August came. The little family had been five months at La Grenadière, and their whole life was changed. The old servant grew anxious and gloomy as she watched the almost imperceptible symptoms of slow decline in the mistress, who seemed to be kept in life by an impassioned soul and intense love of her children. Old Annette seemed to see that death was very near. That mistress, beautiful still, was more careful of her appearance than she had ever been; she was at pains to adorn her wasted self, and wore paint on her cheeks; but often while she walked on the upper terrace with the children, Annette’s wrinkled face would peer out from between the savin trees by the pump. The old woman would forget her work, and stand with wet linen in her hands, scarce able to keep back her tears at the sight of Mme. Willemsens, so little like the enchanting woman she once had been.

===Chinese===

随后她告诉他，她的哀愁和眼泪的一个主因，是想到她死后的第二天，他和玛丽几乎一无依凭，只有一点点薄薄的钱，除了上帝没有一个朋友。
「那我用功必须快些！」路易喊道，给她一个可怜的、探问的眼色。
「哦！我多幸福！」她说，把亲吻和眼泪洒在儿子身上。「他懂我！——路易，」她接下去，「你要做你弟弟的保护人，是不是？你答应我？你不再是孩子了！」
「是，我答应，」他说；「可你还不会死——说你不会死！」
「可怜的小家伙们！」她答道，「对你们的爱系着我的性命。这地方阳光这样好，空气这样爽利，说不定——」
「你叫我比从前更爱都兰了，」孩子说。
从那一天起——那天维莱姆桑夫人预见到死亡的临近，对路易谈了他的将来——他把注意力集中在功课上，愈发勤勉，比从前不爱玩了。等他哄得玛丽肯看书、肯放弃吵闹的游戏以后，石榴居的洼路、园子和台径上就安静了许多。他们把自己的生活去就母亲的忧郁。一天一天，她的脸愈见苍白憔悴，鬓角陷下去了，额上的纹一夜一夜地深。
八月来了。这一小家人在石榴居住了五个月，他们的整个生活变了。老女仆看着女主人那些几乎察觉不出的缓慢衰落的征象，忧惧而阴沉起来——那女主人仿佛全凭一团炽烈的灵魂和对孩子的深爱撑在生命里。老安娜特像是看见死亡已经很近了。那位女主人，依然美丽，比从前更在意自己的仪表；她辛苦地装点那憔悴的自己，颊上施了胭脂；可常常，当她同孩子们在上面台地上散步时，安娜特那张打皱的脸会从水泵边的圆柏丛里探出来。老婆子会忘了手里的活，捏着湿衣裳立在那里，看见维莱姆桑夫人——同她当年那个迷人的女人已经那样不像——几乎忍不住眼泪。

===Original===

The pretty house itself, once so gay and bright, looked melancholy; it was a very quiet house now, and the family seldom left it, for the walk to the bridge was too great an effort for Mme. Willemsens. Louis had almost identified himself, as it were, with his mother, and with his suddenly developed powers of imagination he saw the weariness and exhaustion under the red color, and constantly found reasons for taking some shorter walk.
So happy couples coming to Saint-Cyr, then the Petite Courtille of Tours, and knots of folk out for their evening walk along the “dike,” saw a pale, thin figure dressed in black, a woman with a worn yet bright face, gliding like a shadow along the terraces. Great suffering cannot be concealed. The vinedresser’s household had grown quiet also. Sometimes the laborer and his wife and children were gathered about the door of their cottage, while Annette was washing linen at the wellhead, and Mme. Willemsens and the children sat in the summerhouse, and there was not the faintest sound in those gardens gay with flowers. Unknown to Mme. Willemsens, all eyes grew pitiful at the sight of her, she was so good, so thoughtful, so dignified with those with whom she came in contact.
And as for her.﻿—When the autumn days came on, days so sunny and bright in Touraine, bringing with them grapes and ripe fruits and healthful influences which must surely prolong life in spite of the ravages of mysterious disease﻿—she saw no one but her children, taking the utmost that the hour could give her, as if each hour had been her last.
Louis had worked at night, unknown to his mother, and made immense progress between June and September. In algebra he had come as far as equations with two unknown quantities; he had studied descriptive geometry, and drew admirably well; in fact, he was prepared to pass the entrance examination of the École polytechnique.
Sometimes of an evening he went down to the bridge of Tours. There was a lieutenant there on half-pay, an Imperial naval officer, whose manly face, medal, and gait had made an impression on the boy’s imagination, and the officer on his side had taken a liking to the lad, whose eyes sparkled with energy. Louis, hungering for tales of adventure, and eager for information, used to follow in the lieutenant’s wake for the chance of a chat with him.

===Chinese===

那座漂亮的小宅本身，从前那样明亮欢快，如今也显得忧郁；它如今是一座极安静的宅子，这一家人难得离开它，因为走到大桥去对维莱姆桑夫人已是太费力的事。路易仿佛同母亲合为一体了，凭着他骤然发达的想象力，他看出了那红色下面的疲惫和耗竭，不断找出理由来提议走更近的路线。
于是，来圣西尔——那时是图尔的小库尔蒂耶——散步的幸福伴侣们，和沿「堤」晚游的人群，望见一个苍白瘦削的黑衣身影，一个面容憔悴却明亮的妇人，像一道影子滑过台地。巨大的痛苦是藏不住的。葡萄园工人的一家也静了下来。有时，那劳作者和他的妻儿聚在小屋门口，安娜特在井台边洗衣服，维莱姆桑夫人和孩子们坐在凉亭里，那些鲜花烂漫的园子里没有一丝声音。维莱姆桑夫人不知道，所有的眼睛见了她都生出怜悯，她对谁都是那样好，那样体贴，那样端庄。
至于她自己。——当秋日来临——都兰的秋日那样晴朗明丽，带来葡萄和成熟的果子和有益健康的影响，仿佛必定能延长生命，不顾那种秘疾病的蹂躏——她除了自己的孩子谁也不见，把每个钟头能给的全拿足，仿佛每个钟头都是她的最后一个。
路易背着母亲夜里用功，六月到九月之间进步惊人。代数他已学到两个未知数的方程；他学过画法几何，图画得出色地好；实际上，他已具备了通过综合理工学院入学考试的程度。
有时傍晚他下到图尔大桥去。那里有一个领半薪的海军上尉，一个帝国时代的海军军官，他那张男子汉的脸、勋章和步态在孩子的心里刻下了印象，军官那一面也喜欢上了这个眼睛里闪着劲头的少年。路易渴求冒险的故事，急于求知，常跟在上尉身后，指望同他聊上几句。

===Original===

It so happened that the sailor had a friend and comrade in the colonel of a regiment of infantry, struck off the rolls like himself; and young Louis-Gaston had a chance of learning what life was like in camp or on board a man-of-war. Of course, he plied the veterans with questions; and when he had made up his mind to the hardships of their rough callings, he asked his mother’s leave to take country walks by way of amusement. Mme. Willemsens was beyond measure glad that he should ask; the boy’s astonished masters had told her that he was overworking himself. So Louis went for long walks. He tried to inure himself to fatigue, climbed the tallest trees with incredible quickness, learned to swim, watched through the night. He was not like the same boy; he was a young man already, with a sunburned face, and a something in his expression that told of deep purpose.
When October came, Mme. Willemsens could only rise at noon. The sunshine, reflected by the surface of the Loire, and stored up by the rocks, raised the temperature of the air till it was almost as warm and soft as the atmosphere of the Bay of Naples, for which reason the faculty recommend the place of abode. At midday she came out to sit under the shade of green leaves with the two boys, who never wandered from her now. Lessons had come to an end. Mother and children wished to live the life of heart and heart together, with no disturbing element, no outside cares. No tears now, no joyous outcries. The elder boy, lying in the grass at his mother’s side, basked in her eyes like a lover and kissed her feet. Marie, the restless one, gathered flowers for her, and brought them with a subdued look, standing on tiptoe to put a girlish kiss on her lips. And the pale woman, with the great tired eyes and languid movements, never uttered a word of complaint, and smiled upon her children, so full of life and health﻿—it was a sublime picture, lacking no melancholy autumn pomp of yellow leaves and half-despoiled branches, nor the softened sunlight and pale clouds of the skies of Touraine.
At last the doctor forbade Mme. Willemsens to leave her room. Every day it was brightened by the flowers that she loved, and her children were always with her. One day, early in November, she sat at the piano for the last time.

===Chinese===

碰巧那水手有一个朋友兼战友，是一个步兵团的上校，同他一样被裁了下来；小路易-加斯东便有机会知道军营里和军舰上的生活是什么样。他当然拿问题轰炸两位老兵；等他掂量定了那些粗粝行当的艰辛，便请求母亲准他以乡间远足作为消遣。维莱姆桑夫人见他来请，喜出望外；孩子那些惊讶的教师已经告诉她，他在过度用功。于是路易去做长途的步行。他试炼自己耐得住疲劳，以不可思议的迅捷爬上最高的树，学游泳，彻夜守望。他不像原来那个男孩了；他已经是个青年，一张晒黑的脸，表情里有一种诉说深沉志向的东西。
十月来到时，维莱姆桑夫人只能中午起身了。卢瓦尔河的水面反射的、岩石储存的阳光，把气温抬得几乎同那不勒斯湾一样温暖柔和——为了这个缘故，医学院的先生们推荐这个地方居住。正午她出来坐在绿叶的荫下，同两个男孩在一起——他们如今寸步不离她了。功课结束了。母亲和孩子们要过心贴着心的生活，没有搅扰的成分，没有外界的牵挂。如今没有眼泪，也没有欢快的呼喊。大孩子躺在母亲身边的草里，像一个情人沐浴着她的眼睛，吻她的脚。玛丽，那个不安生的，给她采花，捧着来时带着收敛的神色，踮起脚尖，在她唇上印一个女孩子的吻。那苍白的女人，大大的倦眼，懒懒的动作，从不吐一句抱怨，朝她那充满生命和健康的孩子们微笑——这是一幅崇高的图画，黄色树叶和半已凋落的枝条那悲秋的华彩一样不缺，也不缺都兰的天空那软化的阳光和苍白的云。
末了，医生禁止维莱姆桑夫人离开她的房间。每一天，房间都被她心爱的花照亮，她的孩子们永远在她身边。十一月初的一天，她最后一次坐到钢琴前。

===Original===

A picture﻿—a Swiss landscape﻿—hung above the instrument; and at the window she could see her children standing with their heads close together. Again and again she looked from the children to the landscape, and then again at the children. Her face flushed, her fingers flew with passionate feeling over the ivory keys. This was her last great day, an unmarked day of festival, held in her own soul by the spirit of her memories. When the doctor came, he ordered her to stay in bed. The alarming dictum was received with bewildered silence.
When the doctor had gone, she turned to the older boy.
“Louis,” she said, “take me out on the terrace, so that I may see my country once more.”
The boy gave his arm at those simply uttered words, and brought his mother out upon the terrace; but her eyes turned, perhaps unconsciously, to heaven rather than to the earth, and indeed, it would have been hard to say whether heaven or earth was the fairer﻿—for the clouds traced shadowy outlines, like the grandest Alpine glaciers, against the sky. Mme. Willemsens’ brows contracted vehemently; there was a look of anguish and remorse in her eyes. She caught the children’s hands, and clutched them to a heavily-throbbing heart.
“ ‘Parentage unknown!’ ” she cried, with a look that went to their hearts. “Poor angels, what will become of you? And when you are twenty years old, what strict account may you not require of my life and your own?”
She put the children from her, and leaning her arms upon the balustrade, stood for a while hiding her face, alone with herself, fearful of all eyes. When she recovered from the paroxysm, she saw Louis and Marie kneeling on either side of her, like two angels; they watched the expression of her face, and smiled lovingly at her.
“If only I could take that smile with me!” she said, drying her eyes.
Then she went into the house and took to the bed, which she would only leave for her coffin.
A week went by, one day exactly like another. Old Annette and Louis took it in turns to sit up with Mme. Willemsens, never taking their eyes from the invalid. It was the deeply tragical hour that comes in all our lives, the hour of listening in terror to every deep breath lest it should be the last, a dark hour protracted over many days. On the fifth day of that fatal week the doctor interdicted flowers in the room. The illusions of life were going one by one.

琴的上方挂着一幅画——一幅瑞士风景；窗口她望得见她的孩子们头挨着头站在那里。她一遍又又一次地望望孩子，望望风景，又望望孩子。她脸上泛起红潮，手指带着炽烈的感情在象牙的琴键上飞。这是她最后的一个大日子，一个无人记名的节庆之日，在她自己的灵魂里，由她回忆的精灵主持。医生来时，吩咐她卧床。这个骇人的判词得到的是一片茫然的沉默。
医生走后，她转向那个大孩子。
「路易，」她说，「把我抱到台地上去，好让我再看一眼我的乡土。」
孩子听了这句平平说出的话，伸出手臂，把母亲抱到台地上；可她的眼睛转向的，也许是无意识地，与其说是大地，不如说是天空；真的，也难说天和地哪一样更美——因为云在天空里描出影影绰绰的轮廓，像最壮丽的阿尔卑斯的冰川。维莱姆桑夫人的眉猛烈地蹙起；她眼睛里有一种苦痛和悔恨的神色。她抓住孩子们的手，把它们紧紧按在一颗沉重搏动的心上。
「『父母不详！』」她喊道，那神色直钻进他们的心。「可怜的天使，你们会成为什么人呢？等你们二十岁上，你们对我的生命和你们自己的生命，会怎样地清算啊！」
她推开孩子们，双臂支在栏杆上，立了一会儿，掩着脸，独自对着自己，惧怕一切目光。等她从这一阵激动里缓过来，看见路易和玛丽跪在她两边，像两个天使；他们望着她脸上的表情，爱恋地朝她微笑。
「我若能把这微笑带走多好！」她说，一面拭干眼睛。
随后她进屋上了床——这张床，她除了进棺材，再不离开了。
一个星期过去，每一天同前一天一模一样。老安娜特和路易轮番守着维莱姆桑夫人，眼睛不离病人。那是我们人人生命里都会来的深沉悲怆的时辰：战战兢兢听着每一次深呼吸、生怕它是最后一次的时辰，一道拖过许多天的暗影。那致命的一周的第五天，医生禁止房里再摆花。生命的幻象正一个一个地离去。

Then Marie and his brother felt their mother’s lips hot as fire beneath their kisses; and at last, on the Saturday evening, Mme. Willemsens was too ill to bear the slightest sound, and her room was left in disorder. This neglect for a woman of refined taste, who clung so persistently to the graces of life, meant the beginning of the death-agony. After this, Louis refused to leave his mother. On Sunday night, in the midst of the deepest silence, when Louis thought that she had grown drowsy, he saw a white, moist hand move the curtain in the lamplight.
“My son!” she said. There was something so solemn in the dying woman’s tones, that the power of her wrought-up soul produced a violent reaction on the boy; he felt an intense heat pass through the marrow of his bones.
“What is it, mother?”
“Listen! Tomorrow all will be over for me. We shall see each other no more. Tomorrow you will be a man, my child. So I am obliged to make some arrangements, which must remain a secret, known only to us. Take the key of my little table. That is it. Now open the drawer. You will find two sealed papers to the left. There is the name of **Louis** on one, and on the other **Marie**.”
“Here they are, mother.”
“Those are your certificates of birth, darling; you will want them. Give them to our poor, old Annette to keep for you; ask her for them when you need them. Now,” she continued, “is there not another paper as well, something in my handwriting?”
“Yes, mother,” and Louis began to read, “Marie Willemsens, born at﻿—”
“That is enough,” she broke in quickly, “do not go on. When I am dead, give that paper, too, to Annette, and tell her to send it to the registrar at Saint-Cyr; it will be wanted if my certificate of death is to be made out in due form. Now find writing materials for a letter which I will dictate to you.”
When she saw that he was ready to begin, and turned towards her for the words, they came from her quietly:﻿—

> “Monsieur le Comte, your wife, Lady Brandon, died at Saint-Cyr, near Tours, in the department of Indre-et-Loire. She forgave you.”

「我的儿子！」她说。垂死妇人的声调里有一样那样庄严的东西，她那紧绷的灵魂的力量在孩子身上激起一阵猛烈的震动；他感到一股灼热穿过骨髓。
「什么事，妈妈？」
「听着！明天我的一切就完了。我们再不能相见了。明天你就是大人了，我的孩子。所以我必须做几样安排，它们必须是秘密，只有我们两个知道。拿我小桌子的钥匙。就是它。现在开抽屉。左边你会找到两封封着的纸。一封上写着**路易**，另一封**玛丽**。」
「在这儿，妈妈。」
「那是你们的出生证明，宝贝；你们用得着的。交给我们的老安娜特替你们收着；需要时向她要。现在，」她接下去，「不是还有一张纸么，我的笔迹的什么？」
「是，妈妈，」路易念起来，「玛丽·维莱姆桑，生于——」
「够了，」她急忙打断他，「不要念下去。我死了以后，那张纸也交给安娜特，叫她送到圣西尔的户籍员那里；要按正式格式开我的死亡证明，就用得着它。现在取写信的纸笔来，我念，你写一封信。」
她见他准备动笔、转过脸来等她的话，那些话便安安静静地从她口中出来：——

> 「伯爵先生，您的妻子布兰登夫人，已在安德尔-卢瓦尔省图尔附近的圣西尔去世。她饶恕了您。」

“Sign yourself﻿—” she stopped, hesitating and perturbed.
“Are you feeling worse?” asked Louis.
“Put ‘Louis-Gaston,’ ” she went on.
She sighed, then she went on.
“Seal the letter, and direct it. To Lord Brandon, Brandon Square, Hyde Park, London, Angleterre.﻿—That is right. When I am dead, post the letter in Tours, and prepay the postage.﻿—Now,” she added, after a pause, “take the little pocketbook that you know, and come here, my dear child.﻿ ﻿… There are twelve thousand francs in it,” she said, when Louis had returned to her side. “That is all your own. Oh me! you would have been better off if your father﻿—”
“My father,” cried the boy, “where is he?”
“He is dead,” she said, laying her finger on her lips; “he died to save my honor and my life.”
She looked upwards. If any tears had been left to her, she would have wept for pain.
“Louis,” she continued, “swear to me, as I lie here, that you will forget all that you have written, all that I have told you.”
“Yes, mother.”
“Kiss me, dear angel.”
She was silent for a long while, she seemed to be drawing strength from God, and to be measuring her words by the life that remained in her.
“Listen,” she began. “Those twelve thousand francs are all that you have in the world. You must keep the money upon you, because when I am dead the lawyers will come and seal everything up. Nothing will be yours then, not even your mother. All that remains for you to do will be to go out, poor orphan children, God knows where. I have made Annette’s future secure. She will have an annuity of a hundred crowns, and she will stay at Tours no doubt. But what will you do for yourself and your brother?”
She raised herself, and looked at the brave child, standing by her bedside. There were drops of perspiration on his forehead, he was pale with emotion, and his eyes were dim with tears.
“I have thought it over, mother,” he answered in a deep voice. “I will take Marie to the school here in Tours. I will give ten thousand francs to our old Annette, and ask her to take care of them, and to look after Marie. Then, with the remaining two thousand francs, I will go to Brest, and go to sea as an apprentice. While Marie is at school, I will rise to be a lieutenant on board a man-of-war.

「我想过了，妈妈，」他用一种深沉的嗓音回答。「我带玛丽进图尔的学校。我把一万法郎交给我们的老安娜特，求她照管这笔钱，照看玛丽。然后，拿剩下的两千法郎，我去布雷斯特，上船当见习水手。玛丽上学的时候，我要升到军舰上的军官。

===Original===

There, after all, die in peace, my mother; I shall come back again a rich man, and our little one shall go to the École polytechnique, and I will find a career to suit his bent.”
A gleam of joy shone in the dying woman’s eyes. Two tears brimmed over, and fell over her fevered cheeks; then a deep sigh escaped between her lips. The sudden joy of finding the father’s spirit in the son, who had grown all at once to be a man, almost killed her.
“Angel of heaven,” she cried, weeping, “by one word you have effaced all my sorrows. Ah! I can bear them.﻿—This is my son,” she said, “I bore, I reared this man,” and she raised her hands above her, and clasped them as if in ecstasy, then she lay back on the pillow.
“Mother, your face is growing pale!” cried the lad.
“Someone must go for a priest,” she answered, with a dying voice.
Louis wakened Annette, and the terrified old woman hurried to the parsonage at Saint-Cyr.
When morning came, Mme. Willemsens received the sacrament amid the most touching surroundings. Her children were kneeling in the room, with Annette and the vinedresser’s family, simple folk, who had already become part of the household. The silver crucifix, carried by a chorister, a peasant child from the village, was lifted up, and the dying mother received the Viaticum from an aged priest. The Viaticum! sublime word, containing an idea yet more sublime, an idea only possessed by the apostolic religion of the Roman church.
“This woman has suffered greatly!” the old curé said in his simple way.
Marie Willemsens heard no voices now, but her eyes were still fixed upon her children. Those about her listened in terror to her breathing in the deep silence; already it came more slowly, though at intervals a deep sigh told them that she still lived, and of a struggle within her; then at last it ceased. Everyone burst into tears except Marie. He, poor child, was still too young to know what death meant.
Annette and the vinedresser’s wife closed the eyes of the adorable woman, whose beauty shone out in all its radiance after death. Then the women took possession of the chamber of death, removed the furniture, wrapped the dead in her winding-sheet, and laid her upon the couch.

路易唤醒安娜特，吓坏了的老婆子急急赶到圣西尔的本堂神父宅去。

安娜特和葡萄园工人的妻子阖上这位可爱的人的眼睛，她的美在死后焕发出全部的光彩。随后女人们接过这间死亡的卧室，搬开家具，给死者裹上殓衣，把她安放在长榻上。

They lit tapers about her, and arranged everything﻿—the crucifix, the sprigs of box, and the holy-water stoup﻿—after the custom of the countryside, bolting the shutters and drawing the curtains. Later the curate came to pass the night in prayer with Louis, who refused to leave his mother. On Tuesday morning an old woman and two children and a vinedresser’s wife followed the dead to her grave. These were the only mourners. Yet this was a woman whose wit and beauty and charm had won a European reputation, a woman whose funeral, if it had taken place in London, would have been recorded in pompous newspaper paragraphs, as a sort of aristocratic rite, if she had not committed the sweetest of crimes, a crime always expiated in this world, so that the pardoned spirit may enter heaven. Marie cried when they threw the earth on his mother’s coffin; he understood that he should see her no more.
A simple, wooden cross, set up to mark her grave, bore this inscription, due to the curé of Saint-Cyr:﻿—

> Here lies

**an unhappy woman**,

who died at the age of thirty-six.
> Known in Heaven by the name of Augusta.
> *Pray for her!*
